speechtext:
its Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities. But, if the Government is to relieve the Grand Trunk Company of liabilities which it voluntarily incurred, but which it now finds it impossible to meet, it is for the Government, not for the company, to fix the terms.
I imagine this is the road, the acquisition of which the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. I). Reid) had in mind the other day when he said that he believed the day was not far distant when the Government railways would be able to pay operating expenses and take care of fixed charges as well. I think the expression he used was that he could almost see ahead where he was going to turn the corner. There is an old saying that "fools rush in where angels fear to tread." Of course, I do not wish to put the Minister of Railways in that class at all, because I do not believe he is in that class, but I do want to warn him not to turn that corner at too high a rate of speed, especially if he is heading in the same direction as he has been doing in connection with the Canadian Government railways for the last two or three years at least. I am afraid he might run into something; he might even meet himself coming back. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I do not think it is the matter of acquiring railways that is so important; the important matter is how you acquire them and if you are getting value for the money you put into the undertaking. What I object to is the limit which the Government has set on the amount the arbitrators shall find as compensation to the shareholders or whoever we are getting this white elephant from. The Government sets a limit that the arbitrators shall not go above a limit which will amount to $64,666,666.66. I could hardly understand all the sixes. If they had been sevens, I might have understood them because seven is supposed to be a lucky number. But they say that the fixing of this limit has nothing whatever to do with the determining of the award. I quote from the agreement:	'
The fixing of this limit shall not be taken by the arbitrators as an admission or indication that the value to be determined is the amount so fixed or any other amount.
In the case of the Canadian Northern I believe that the limit of the valuation to be arrived at by the Board of Arbitrators was $10,000,000; yet the award was $10,800,000, in round figures. Have we any reason to believe that the same will not happen in this case? In view of the result of the investigation made into the railway situation by a person of such eminent ability as our present Finance Minister (Sir Henry Dray-

ton)-I do not know so well the other member of that commission, but I have every reason to believe that he was a man of considerable ability-I cannot reconcile my conscience to approving the acquirement of this road on the terms stated.
The Minister of Justice told us this afternoon that this agreement was arrived at during a previous session of Parliament and that all we were asked to do now was to ratify that agreement. I was in the House at that time but I was not permitted to take part in the discussion; I was permitted only to sit in the gallery. There also are other members of the House who are here now but who were not here at that time. Had there been a sufficient number of by-elections since that time, there would be enough members here at the present time to now prevent the acquirement of the Grand Trunk on the terms proposed. My reason for discussing the matter at this time is that I did not have an opportunity to discuss it when the matter was before the House last fall, nor an opportunity to vote on it, therefore I did not feel like letting this occasion pass without putting my views on record in regard to the whole matter of the acquisition of this road as well as the building of the Transcontinental.

It may" be interesting to the hon. member (Mr. Caldwell) to hear a quotation from the London Times in which some remarks made by Sir Alfred Smithers are published with regard to what the earnings of the Grand Trunk Railway system would have been if a sufficient or reasonable increase in freight rates was allowed. The report says:
But it may be urged on behalf of the Government that I have taken no account of our Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities; well, for reasons which I have often explained, X do not think it is fair or right we should have those liabilities forced upon us. i will say something on that in a moment, but the fact is, even if those liabilities had been enforced, we should with the requisite increase of freight rates have earned sufficient in 1916, 1917, 1918 and 1919 to have taken care of our Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities.
The hon. member is apparently misinformed, as he would have every cause to be from the statements made in the public press and the assertions of members of the Government, with regard to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental. His contention that the cost of the road was estimated at $61,000,000 is quite correct. The road was being built through what was practically a

wilderness. It was opening up new territory at a time when Canada was most prosperous and when the prices of everything were going up. I may also point out to the hon. member that the National Transcontinental was built out of the revenues of the country, not out of borrowings as we are proposing to do in this case.
Oh, oh.
That is a fact which cannot be disputed. It is absolutely true and every member opposite knows that it is true.
Not at all.

The road was being built out of the revenues of the day. But when the then Government went out of power they left so much money that my hon. friends who took office did not know what to do with it. But since the present Government spent that money they never have had a cent; they were not able to accumulate any more.
There was an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of that day to operate the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The cost of the road was a matter of arrangement between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, a company that was well financed at that time, in good condition and having sufficient backing to fulfil its obligation to the Government of Canada. It was not a lame duck like the Canadian Northern; it was well able to operate the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Speaking to his directors not two months ago Mr. Smithers contended that with a fair increase in rates the Grand Trunk would still be able to take care of the obligations under the agreement to which I have referred. The present Government did not insist upon the Grand Trunk living up to their agreement; they simply took over the road and let it go at that, and they have since been consistently working to kill the road. I pointed out here a few days ago that 6.500 carloads of material in one section of the Transcontinental had not been moved because there were no cars. The minister said that these shipments were destined for American points. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker. I have a letter from one of the best informed men in the district, Mr. Authier, a land agent who travels up and down the country and knows the conditions well and he tells me that Beven-ty-five per cent of the cars of wood and lumber to be shipped from the points along that territory are for Canadian points, 84*
largely in Ontario, and not for American points. But it has been the studied policy of the Government to condemn in every way the building of the National Transcontinental and to make its operation a failure if possible.
The minister pointed out in his statement that the Transcontinental was losing only $2,750,000. If the same settlement was permitted along the Transcontinental west of Cochrane that is taking place on the Transcontinental east of Cochrane in the province of Quebec, the Transcontinental would pay its way to-day, but owing to the policy of the Ontario Department of Colonization the country is a wilderness from Quebec to Cochrane. The Government should see to it that proper settlers are allowed to settle in that territory and thus develop traffic for the road.
I am not here to defend the late Liberal administration for their railway policy, but I will say that this Government have spent more money on railways in the last two years and got less for it than the Liberal administration spent during the whole fifteen years they were in power. That is a fact that cannot be denied. The Government have spent over $200,000,000 during the last two years and they have yet a deficit of $47,000,000 to meet. At a time when the country was prosperous, when we had good administration of the country's affairs and when the building of railways went hand in hand with the promotion of immigration and colonization, the Liberal administration were justified in believing that they might open up new territory. But unfortunately for the people of Canada my hon. friends opposite came into power and began to tear down. They were too prosperous; they had too much money. They were inexperienced in, handling the affairs of the country, and they have since shown no inclination to learn; at least they have shown no inclination to save the people's money.
When the Liberal administration were in power they insisted that the Canadian Northern should not build to the Coast through the Rockies. There was a Conservative administration in power in British Columbia and they guaranteed the bonds. It is true that there was a duplication of trackage between the Great Lakes and the East, but a great part of that country is a splendid country if properly developed under a policy of putting people on the land instead of being retarded under a protectionist policy that is driving the peop.le
to the cities. If you get the popular

They will not open
those that should be opened.

No; and they would not attempt to go to the country on the question of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. I think they would be very chary about testing public opinion on this or any other *question in which the people are interested. I am positive, and I am sure the *country is with me in this, that public ownership of railways in Canada cannot possibly be a success while the McKenzie and Mann crowd are handling affairs. The people of the country are not in favour of taking over the Grand Trunk to be handed over to McKenzie and Mann for their management, and I say that the Government does not represent the wishes of the Canadian people in regard to this matter. As pointed out by my hon. friend from Joliette, the agreement was not lived up to by tne Grand Trunk people, and of this fact I do not think there can be any doubt at all. As a matter of fact no one is affected except the Government, the Mckj*r. UClIll.]
Kenzie and Mann interests, and some of the other interests that are making money out of the Grand Trunk stocks. They are the only people who are interested in this transaction and are anxious to have it consummated. The Canadian people would not suffer by a delay, and, as regards the shareholders of the Grand Trunk, I should like to read a remarkable resolution passed at the meeting, as reported in the London Times. This resolution will reflect the feeling of the shareholders:
Mr. Grant Hooper said that the resolution proposed by the chairman having now been carried, he wished to submit the following resolution : " That this meeting, though accepting the agreement imposed upon the company by the Government, protests against the treatment to which the company has been subjected in being refused permission adequately to increase rates, and in the limitation of the amount of uic arbitration award."
Mr. Ince seconded this, and it was carried unanimously.
The only resolutions that were carried unanimously at the meeting of the shareholders were those opposed to the acquisition of the railway by this Government. It is quite evident '.that there was strong opposition on the part of the shareholders, and Mr. Smithers stated that the Government was forcing them to accept the bargain. As they could do nothing else under the circumstances they decided that they would have to accept it, but they immediately began to pass resolutions condemning the attitude of the Canadian Government, and declared that, under fair conditions, they could earn dividends and pay their liabilities towards the Grand Trunk Pacific. When we get into committee-which I trust we shall not-I purpose to ask the Minister of Railways how much additional deficit he will expect to have next year over and above the deficit of this year. He told us that there was a deficit of $47,000,000 on the roads that were being operated, and I .shall be anxious to know how much additional deficit the Grand Trunk will add to our present heavy obligations. *Now, if the people of Canada do not want the road-and I have no doubt that they do not-I think that the Government, instead of asking Parliament to jam this legislation through, ratifying an agreement about which we know nothing, should go back to the Grand Trunk shareholders and let them accept or refuse it as they choose. There is nothing to be lost by the people of Canada. Last year, it is true, there were a number of people who seemed to think that the acquisition of the Grand Trunk was going to help the National rail-

ways, and that there was going to be some sort of capable management instituted. The majority of the people, however, I regret to say, have lost all confidence in my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Reid), and do not believe that he will do anything but what he is doing to-day,-virtually maintaining McKenzie and Mann in control of the treasury of Canada. These interests are enabled to tap the public treasury, by the railway policy of the present administration, and by this transaction they are going to be given further access to the pockets of the people, who will get no benefit whatever in return for the public moneys that will be spent. There is another question to which I shall expect an answer when we are in committee. The Times says:
The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried by an overwhelming majority, only six hands being held up against it.
I do not understand how a vote of that nature could be taken by a show of hands, because there would be no way of ascertaining what stocks were being voted on in that way. The report goes on to say:
The chairman appealed to the dissentients to give him a unanimous vote, but they still declined to vote for the resolution.
The solicitor (Mr. Profit) said that the resolution was carried, but they required to know, for the purpose of the records in Canada, the amount of stock represented by the dissentient votes. The chairman observed that there was an overwhelming majority in the room, and also in the proxies, in favour of the resolution, and all that was desired now was to satisfy a technical point.
I suppose that that is what we are trying to do now.
Sir Charles Russell was present, as representing the Canadian Government, and he had to satisfy himself that the gentlemen who dissented were in a minority. There was no doubt about it, but still they must have it in black and white. It would therefore be a convenience if the half-dozen members who voted against the resolution would hand in their names so that their holdings might be ascertained.
I do not see anything in the correspondence laid on the Table yesterday as to the amount of the votes represented in the dissentients. But the point is that we are asked to ratify an agreement which the people of Canada do not want, and against which I desire to go on record as being absolutely opposed. I protest against the whole transaction as strenuously as I can, because I believe it to be a bad bargain, a bargain that is not in any sense in the interests of the Canadian people.

I do not know where
the statement originated but it could only have originated through Mr. Hinton himself or Mr. Kelley, President of the- Grand Trunk. I am not trying to force out anybody but I am exceedingly anxious that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian National shall be joined together and shall be operated together at as early a moment as possible. If we continue operating the Grand Trunk Pacific separately from the Canadian National we will have a loss probably equal to what we have this year unless there is a change of rates or we have a larger crop or something of that kind which may affect the result. If we can put these two railways together there will be a great saving. When we get this Bill through and get these two railways together it will be for the management of the Canadian National railways to say whether they are

going to continue the operation of the two Railways in the way they are being carried on now. Mr. Warren is general manager of eight or nine thousand miles of railways west of the Great Lakes and Mr. Hinton is general manager of the Grand Trunk Pa-* cific. You cannot possibly economize in any way and allow the present system oi management to continue. I did say to Mr. Hinton and Mr. Kelley that just as soon [DOT] as -I -can be relieved of the responsibility oi carrying on the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific I will have it transferred to the Canadian National railways and allow them to continue the operation. Would the hon. gentleman, if he were in my position, wish to continue the whole staff and have two managers for one railway? Either one manager or the other would have to sever his connection with these railways. My opinion is that Mr. Warren, who has charge of the Canadian National lines, who has always been an operating man and who is considered by hon. members who know him to be one of the ablest of the younger operators in Canada, would be expected to be the man who would take charge of the operation of these united railways. I will be very sorry if Mr. Hinton has to retire from his position but if the services of Mr. Hinton or any other man of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway have to be dispensed with I hope we shall be in a position to see that Mr. Hinton and any other man who is able to continue in the service shall be tatken care *of by the Grand Trunk Railway system. Could I do more? I think that is fair. When we get this agreement through and when we are amalgamating these two railways and trying to economize, if it is necessary that men must sever their connection with the road, the fault is not mine. It must fall upon the management of the consolidated railways and not upon me. I really feel that it is in the interest of the country to try and get the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian National railways together at the earliest possible moment and economize in every way. I have been told by the management of the Canadian National railways that if you can put them together you can save at least $500,000 per annum and perhaps a very much larger amount.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
There is no person questioning the efficiency of Mr. Warren but the statement we want to bring out from the minister is one as to who is running this road. Is it the committee or is it the minister? The minister has given the reply himself; he says he proposes putting Mr. 
Warren, an old Canadian Northern Railway man, into the position to replace Mr. Hinton. The minister has given evidence that the only person who is going to manage the road is the Minister of Railways and Canals.

In regard to the question which the minister has raised about efficiency in the Canadian railways I would like to know if he is aware of the fact that in so far as cars "are concerned, the whole system has broken down in the asbestos districts of the eastern townships. The car shortage is so-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must call my hon.
friend to order. The car shortage in the Eastern Townships is certainly not relevant to the clause now before the committee for the purpose of amending the schedule of the Grand Trunk Railway Act.
Mr. Chairman, let me say that it has as much to do with the section under consideration as the address which has just been made by the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The address just made by the minister was a reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). The rule is very clear, that all discussions in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the clause under consideration. If the committee gives its unanimous consent, the hon. gentleman may proceed with his remarks. Without such unanimous consent the hon. gentleman may not proceed. Is it the unanimous consent of the committee that the hon. gentleman be allowed to proceed?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Without the unanimous consent of the committee I must apply the rule.
I am sure the committee will give the unanimous consent.
Am I to understand, Mr. Chairman, by your ruling that the remarks made by the minister were in order and that my remarks were not?
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must point out to
the hon. member that a ruling from the Chair cannot be questioned.
It is not being questioned or discussed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. gentleman's question I may say this:	If
the answering of one question, not strictly

in conformity with the rule, should be taken as a precedent and be acted upon by other hon. members, the business of the committee could not possibly be advanced. I am very sorry indeed that it should fall to the lot of the hon. member to be the first to be called to order. However, the line must be drawn somewhere, and the Chairman felt compelled to rule as he did.

All I can say is that the
minister made a slip and I am called to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The only slip made by the minister was an answer to a question asked by an hon. member of the Opposition which should not have been allowed by the Chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the minister if he is aware of the meeting of Grand Trunk shareholders to be held in London on the 29th of this month, to which the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has alluded?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The notice read here to-day was the first intimation I had of that meeting.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In view of the fact that the minister is now aware of the meeting does he consider it necessary to proceed with this legislation? Would it not be possible for the shareholders to agree to the changes which are desired, if they are willing to do so?

I do not think the leader of the Opposition was in the Chamber when the Minister of Justice explained that it would not be possible to have this agreement disposed of at that particular meeting. In other words, a special meeting would have to be called, and the shareholders would have to be notified that it was a special meeting called for that particular purpose.
If there was time to call a general meeting, there was also time to call a special meeting.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I was merely answering a question put to me by the leader of the Opposition.

Before this clause
passes I think it would be useful to place before the committee the manner in which the more than generous offer made by the Canadian Government to the Grand Trunk shareholders was received by those shareholders. From time to time I have seen
extracts in our papers which gave me some inkling of the way these gentlemen were talking. Last year I protested with all my force against the adoption of this relation with the Grand Trunk. I thought that the shareholders, especially some classes of them, were being treated far too kindly. My own feeling was that if the Grand Trunk was unable to meet its obligations, whether those obligations were connected with the old parent company or the Grand Trunk Pacific, they should be allowed to go into liquidation, that a receiver should be appointed, and then if it was wise for the Government to buy from the receiver that course should be adopted. The Government, as an objection to this proposal, said it would hurt our credit in the Old Country. Under the circumstances let me read what the shareholders of the Grand Trunk have been saying in the Old Country to see whether, by the improvident bargain we made last year, we have in any way increased Canadian prestige overseas.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman proceeds to do so I would ask him to connect his remarks with the clause under consideration? I think that they would be quite in order under clause 2, but certainly not under this clause.

The man whose remarks I am going to quote is a shareholder in this company in connection with which we are asked to correct this agreement. It seems to roe that I am in order, but if you prefer that I should delay my remarks until the next clause is reached, I only live while I am in the House to obey the ruling of the Speaker, or the chairman of the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's remarks would be more in order on clause 2. Shall clause 1 carry?
Mr. McKENZIE,: Can the minister give us any idea as to the length and financial standing of the new railroads that we are taking in and dealing with? Are they large or small railways, and are they earning dividends and conducting a good business? Are they to be tributary to the rest of the system, and what generally is the standing of these properties that we are taking power to acquire?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The Vermont and Province Railroad Company, the stock of which we now own one hundred per cent, is, I think, 3.16 miles in length. The other line, the Pembroke Southern railway, was mentioned in the schedule of the Act last

year, only it was stated that it was controlled by lease, whereas we actually control the stock ownership. It is twenty-one miles in length and that really does not affect the question at all.
Is it a branch line, and if so, of which road?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Pembroke Southern is a branch of the Canada Atlantic railway. When the Grand Trunk took over the Canada Atlantic system this was a branch line, some twenty-one miles in length. The other line is a branch of the Central Vermont, a small spur line.

Is the Pembroke
Southern conducted as a separate entity, or is it operated as a branch of the Canada Atlantic?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is a subsidiary company and operated as part of the Canada Atlantic system of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It runs from Pembroke to Golden Lake. ,
As a matter of management and of ascertaining its earning capacity and maintenance cost, is it treated as a separate entity or as an integral part of the main system?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not suppose there would be any difficulty in getting an approximate estimate of the earnings and expenses of this particular branch line, but this being a short line operated as part of the whole system it does not strike me that the information asked for is of any serious importance when we are merely correcting an error.
The only reason I am asking for the information is that when* we reach schedule 1 specifying the seventy-four lines to be taken over, we may require full details.

Could the minister tell
us who is president of this three miles of railway we are having so much difficulty in taking over?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Mr. Kelley is the president. The president of the Grand Trunk is also appointed president of these subsidiary companies.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is the minister sure of that information? Is not Mr. Smith, of St. Albans, the president?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We are talking of the Pembroke line.
No, I was speaking of the Vermont and Province line.	[DOT]*

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I saw it stated in the press that this Vermont line had its own officials, but I could not say at the moment. If the hon. member thinks it is of sufficient importance, I can telephone for the information between now and eight o'clock.

Will the hon. gentleman
tell us whether the cars of the Vermont and Province line are owned by the Grand Tiunk?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: All these branch lines are owned and controlled by the Grand Trunk, and this ownership of control would of course cover the equipment.
Would the Grand Trunk officials have any power to order these cars into the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Any cars on their own road they would bring into the country; they are operating in that way.
At six o'clock the House resumed and then took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext: I may point out to my hon. friend that the introduction of the list of these roads into the agreement was only to comply with section 2 of the Act of last session which required that the agreement should contain provision for the defining of the company's properties and interests comprised in the Grand Trunk system, and we are dealing merely with an error in the list. The purpose of that defining is not to determine, nor are we determining in any way, what effect the ownership of these roads by the Grand Trunk, or the ownership of whatever rights they have in connection with them, will have on the value. That will be for the Board of Arbitrators to decide, and the only necessity for the mention of these roads is the fact that in the agreement we are obliged to have a definition of all these things. But their liabilities or their assets can have no bearing on the subject-matter of this particular Bill. The arbitrators will have to consider all these things when they deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
What the minister has said may be all right, but we have discovered since last session that there was an error in the Bill and the case is now all under review, and the people have a right to know what obligations we are assuming. Last year when the question was before Parliament the attention of the Minister of Railways was called to the fact that the capital stock of the Central Vermont Railway was $2,984,600, of which the Grand Trunk Railway owns $2,191,100. The outstanding funded debt is $11,750,000, the Grand Trunk Railway guaranteeing interest in bonds providing for deficiency up to 30 per cent of the gross receipts. What I want to call the attention of the minister to particularly is the fact that the Central Vermont Railway guarantees $200,000 worth of bonds of the Vermont and Province Line, and the Central Vermont Railway owns the stock and bonds of the Southern New England railway, which was partly built in and projected from Palmer, Massachusetts, to Providence, Rhode Island. This line has been abandoned and a suit is now pending for $3,000,000. The whole subject is under review to-night, since the minister has introduced a part of the Central Vermont railway, and this is an opportune time for him to make a statement as to how the citizens

of Canada will be affected if this suit goes against us. Will Canada be called upon to take up the defence that is now being conducted by the Central Vermont Railway on behalf of the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
That suit has nothing to do with the particular errors we are correcting. Any suit or claim for damages against the Grand Trunk Railway will, of course, be taken into consideration by the arbitrators when the award is made.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	We are guaranteeing
the interest on many debentures and assuming heavy financial responsibilities with which the award has nothing to do. Even if there should never be any award we are still assuming great responsibilities, and the minister must not forget that fact. When the subject was before us last year we asked the Government to be considerate enough to submit the agreement to Parliament before sending it across to the old country, so that we might have an opportunity of examining it before it became a closed book. The minister will remember that we were denied that right, and it is only by a sort of providential accident that the thing is here now. We have the right to inquire into its contents and ask for as much information as we can possibly obtain in regard to it. If we are not permitted to do that, then it is childish to submit the agreement to this 'House. The agreement is now before us for the very first time, and it is only reasonable that hon. members should ask for information concerning it. The minister must not assume that there is any attempt to impose upon him or obstruct the passage of the Bill, but we submit that he should be prepared to give us all the information that he possibly can. If the minister says that he did not anticipate these questions, then I think it would be well for us to take time so that he may obtain the information that is sought.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

which I cannot answer to-night, and which the committee insists upon, I will have to give it at a subsequent sitting.

We have a copy of the agreement which has been distributed to members of Parliament. That copy shows, on page 8, amongst the roads controlled by the Central Vermont Railway, 'the Montreal and Province Line Railway Company. The Bill now before us reads:
Vermont and Province Line Railroad Company, controlled by stock ownership,-100 per cent.
Is there a Vermont and Province Line Railroad Company as well as a Montreal and Province Line Railroad Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.

The Montreal and
Southern Counties Railway Company is the company whose Bill we passed this evening for an extension of time. That came up in the Railway Committee yesterday, I think. That is a railway running from Montreal to Granby. There is this other railway in addition to that.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: There is no reference whatever in this agreement to the road the minister has described. Is this for the purpose of adding the Vermont and Province line railway to the schedule of last year? The schedule of last year gave a list of the railways but this one was not in.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.

Mr. Chairman, I think
it would ibe a good idea if the minister in charge of this Bill would divide it into two sections, send half of it down to this end of the Chamber and let us discuss it here. It is utterly impossible for us to understand what is going on at the other end of the Chamber.
Mr. CALDWEiLL:	If the hon. member
for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) is making that as a motion I would be pleased to second it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Before recess the minister said that he was rather anxious to take possession of the Grand 'Trunk because he expected it would enable him to improve the earnings of the other lines which belong to the Government. Will the accounts of each company be kept separately so that at the end of the year the country will be in a position to know what the earnings of each line have been?
Mr. J. D. 'REID: It has been the custom of all railways, not only the Canadian Northern,-the Canadian National as it is now-.but the Canadian Pacific, to keep a record of the different branches so that they shall know what their earnings are. But even if they do this it hardly shows the true position. The branch lines are feeders. The traffic that the main line gets from a branch line adds to the earnings of the railway as a whole and while the earnings of the branch line itself may bear a small proportion to the earnings of the main line as a whole and while the branch line may haul the traffic at a loss, yet the business shows a profit when you take into consideration the long haul. subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Will there be a balance
sheet for the Intercolonial, the Quebec and Saguenay, the Grand Trunk, and the Canadian Northern?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: These as well as the Grand Trunk Pacific will be kept separately.

I am amazed that my hon. friend considers compliance with the statute law of this country to be absolutely superfluous. What I pointed out was that a thing may be useful, though it does not bear on some particular matter; and a correct definition of the property and interests comprised in the Grand Trunk system was thought by Parliament last year to be a useful thing to be annexed to this agreement, and Parliament enacted that it should be so annexed. subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: While in theory my hon. friend's statement about our desire to own this stock is right, in practice and for the purpose that Parliament had in view in acquiring this road, it is not strictly correct. It is useless for the Government, and more especially it is useless for the Minister of Justice, to endeavour rto convince the people of Canada thajt we are mere stockholders ; that we are merely a nation which has money to invest in stock; that we have invested that money in the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and after we have made the investment we shall complacently sit back and wait until we get dividends. That is pot the correct situation. In one way it is-that is, we are acquiring the stock. Whait are the responsibilities of a man who acquires stock in any corporation? He pays for the stock whatever the price is; he puts the stock in his strong box in the bank or in his safe, if he has one, and then he waits until he receives dividends on (that stock or until he hears that there is to be no dividend. That is the situation in regard to any stockholder in any limited liability company. Is that the condition here? We have millions of stock in this concern, and when the end of the year comes there is no dividend; on the contrary, there is a huge deficit up in the millions of dollars. Who pays that deficit? Will my hon. friend and all the Test of the members of the House say: Oh, well, it is nothing to us that the road is in debt and is not paying its way; it is true we have the stock, but let the company look about them for money with which to run the road. What will happen is that the treasury of Canada and the people of Canada will pay the debt. Can it be said, in view of those circumstances, that we are mere stockholders in this concern? The situation is more complex than that. We take the stock merely as a means of getting the physical assets of this road under our management and control; we pay for the stock, and we shall pay for the running of the road, and we shall also pay the deficits; so that we are in an entirely different position from that of the ordinary stockholder. I am sure nobody understands that better than the Minister of Justice, and it would be just as well to tell the Canadian people candidly that they are not merely stockholders, but owners of the physical assets of the road, and that if it does not pay it is the Canadian people who will have to make good the deficit.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
There are necessarily
two parties or more to an agreement. In this case, there are two; the party of the first part is the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada of which the Government is a committee; the party of the second part is the Grand Trunk Railway Company with its associated and subsidiary companies and the various financial groups with which it Is associated and which have more or less power in connection with the management of its affairs. We, the party of the first part, have made a blunder. When I say "we," I use that expression in the sense that we are all responsible for the acts of Parliament. Whether we agree with them or not, we have to bow to the judgment of the majority, and we are all jointly responsible for the conclusions that are reached. The Government and the Parliament of Canada have made a mistake, which at one stage of the discussion was spoken of-as a matter of little or no importance, and which, at another stage, we were reminded, was a matter of grave concern. Whether the blunder be great or small, it is a blunder for which we are responsible, and we, the Government and Parliament of Canada, can properly be called upon to make good that blunder. That is what is

done by the first clause of the Bill, and to that extent I quite agree -with hon. gentlemen opposite that we are taking a proper course.
I come to the question of the party of the second part, which is the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the various companies consolidated with it, with their varying greater or lesser voting power. Has this company fulfilled its part? Has it carried out the intention of the law? Eminent counsel in England representing the Grand Trunk Railway Company have said that it has, and eminent counsel representing the *Government of Canada say the same. We have run up a bill of legal expenses that, I have no doubt, will amount to thousands of dollars, and Whether in the first instance that is paid by the Grand Trunk Railway Company or by anybody else, it is pretty safe to venture the statement that in the end the treasury of Canada will foot the bill. All these legal expenses have resulted in the conclusion that this company has performed its part all right. If that be correct, why should, we go any further? But, says the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), there is a doubt; that is, he says, I cannot admit a doubt myself, but somebody has suggested that there is a doubt; the old Great Western of Canada, which was consolidated years ago with the Grand Trunk had certain rights in the la/tter company, and it is said that some of the shareholders of that concern were not properly notified, and that, in consequence of that or of some other minor irregularity, these proceedings are invalid and the proceedings of the so-called meeting in London have no legal effect at all. I am not endorsing that view, nor saying that it is correct, but is this a matter in which the Parliament of Canada should presume to interfere? We should interfere to correct our own blunders, but we have no right to come and declare that something the company has done, which is a matter of dispute, is a legal and valid bargain, because that is a matter for the company to deal with. If it is all right, let it stand at that. If it is all wrong, we must leave the company to make good the error by its own act and in its own way. It is not the duty of this Parliament to declare something in the name of the company when we are told that members of the company or of interests connected with it are dissatisfied with the proceedings. The Minister of Justice said-and I think ithe Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) said the same thing-this does not make any difference, because if all thest parties had

been present and had voted against the resolution, the result would have been just the same. I am surprised that a lawyer would use that argument. The question whether this would make a difference in votes cannot make any difference in regard to the legality of the proceeding. If the thing is legal and valid, the question of votes does not affect it in any way.
There is this other view that I might mention. It may very well be contended that it is conceivable, if these parties had been present and if they had the plausibility of my esteemed friend the Minister of Justice, they might have been able to persuade all those other stockholders that they were wrong. Therefore, I do not think the question whether they were few ox many affects this matter at all. While it is right and proper that we should correct our own blunder, it would be a highly improper procedure for us to undertake to say that something which was done by the company in London and which appears to the Government of Canada to be a matter of dispute, was a valid proceeding. Let the company, if the proceeding was a defective one, correct it, just as we must be left to correct our own mistakes. That is the proper course to adopt. I have alfeady referred to the point raised by the Minister of Railways as to the delay that would take place, and I have pointed out that while we have been debating this matter the company have called a meeting; and if they have called one meeting by a notice inserted in the Canada Gazette, there would be no difficulty in calling a meeting in another manner if that were necessary, so that they might do in a proper manner what we are being asked to do here in violation of all sound legal procedure. I am going to ask the Government to be content with correcting the error for which we are responsible. I therefore respectfully move that clause 2 be amended by striking out all the words after the word " agreement " in the first line thereof and substituting therefor the following words r
-as hereby corrected, shall be as binding and effective as it would have been if the alterations set forth in the first section of this Act had been made in the schedule at the time the agreement was executed.
We say that so far as we made a mistake in omitting the names of these companies, we correct our error; but if the company has made any mistake; if the comlpany has been guilty of any neglect; if the company has failed in any respect to carry out the provisions and intentions of the Act for the

acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway system, we must leave it to the company to make good; we must not undertake to make good for them.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.

The hon. gentleman
premises his argument by an argument based upon the statement that the Government of Canada made one blunder and the Grand Trunk Railway Company another, and he conceives that it belongs to the Government to propose legislation such as may be necessary to correct its blunder. But we are going entirely out of our way, he says, going beyond what it is right for us to do, to correct what he calls the blunder of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
If it was a blunder.
Let me in the first place point out that so far as there have been blunders, if we may so call them, neither of them are attributable to the Government of Canada. The definition of the property and interests of the Grand Trunk Railway Company must necessarily come from the company itself Now, I would not speak of it as a blunder. Through an error, the officers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in making this list omitted the -name of one bit of road three miles long, and in the case of another road erroneously stated - the nature of their interest in it. If that is to be called a " blunder," it was the " blunder" of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. If there -was any irregularity in the calling of the meeting and if we are going to call that a blunder, that, too, was the blunder of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It was calling this meeting for the purpose of enabling its shareholders to ratify this agreement. It had control of the procedure of calling that meeting. So far I agree with the hon. gentleman that if what happened in that respect is to be called a blunder it was the blunder of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. But as he himself has pointed out, the Grand Trunk Railway Company does not admit that there was any irregularity or any blunder. They say: We have held a perfectly proper meeting under the statute and have therefore completely complied with our agreement. As the hon. gentleman has. also pointed out, counsel on behalf of the Government are disposed to share that opinion. That being so, shall we say to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which itself contends it has committed no error:	"You gentlemen must
get together; you must call another meeting"? If the doubt that has been 85
raised is not settled that doubt will lead to the prejudice of the owners of the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, that is to say, to the prejudice of the people of this country. This question has been raised as a question that suggests a doubt whether the title that is given to the people of this country under this agreement will be a valid title. Who is most interested in having that doubt settled? 'Is it the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, who are parting with their stock, or is it those who are acquiring the stock? Who is it in any purchase of property who is interested in seeing that the title is beyond question? Of course, it is the purchaser; it is the acquirer. In every transaction for the acquisition of property is it the vendor who goes hunting round to find out whether or not his title is perfectly good or whether the title he has given the other man is perfectly good? Why, it is the purchaser who is anxious to satisfy himself, first, that the vendor had a good title, and, second, that the instrument by which the vendor is conveying it to him gives him a valid and effective title. In the opinion of counsel for the Grand Trunk Railway Company and of counsel for the Government the question that is raised does not affect the validity of the title. We are agreed upon that, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company naturally says: I have neither interest nor obligation to clear away whatever cloud may exist as against that title that you are going to acquire by reason of the fact that some counsel has suggested a possible doubt. It is the result of the action of the Parliament of Canada that the acquisition is made. As the hon. gentleman has very properly pointed out, it is not a question of who voted for it or who voted against it; it is the action of Parliament that brings about this acquisition. The Government feel that inasmuch as we are the agents and representatives of the people in the acquisition of this stock, it behooves us to see to it that the people get a title upon which there shall be no cloud. If there be suggested to a purchaser a doubt as to the validity of his title to a property, does he sit back in calm repose and say: Well, my vendor's counsel says it is all right and my lawyer is convinced that it is all right? No, he will say: Some people think that there may be a question of the validity of my title; I will take proper and effective methods to quiet that doubt. All of us who have had to do with titles know what steps are taken to quiet such doubts. Now, this is what we are asking Parliament to do, in the



interests of the people of Canada and with no risk of doing injustice to anybody. The real effect of this enactment is to leave the people of Canada with a title safe from any attack upon the basis of a doubt which rests upon purely technical grounds. That is the position; it is very clear and very simple. What can we be reproached for? When we ask Parliament to give an afternoon of its time to do that which will remove this possible cloud upon the title of the people of Canada, is it an entirely useless trouble? Would not any one of us take just as much trouble for the purpose of making clear beyond peradventure the title to property that we were acquiring? That is the whole mystery that is involved in this matter, and I confess that I am surprised that it should be suggested that we were taking an extraordinary amount of trouble to do something which it is said the Grand Trunk Railway Company ought to d.o.
Of course, if the mistake be the Grand Trunk Railway Company's admitted mistake they ought to correct it. But Parliament lias decided that it is in the interests of the people of this country to acquire this road, and therefore it is our duty to carry out the mandate of Parliament given at its last session, and to carry the agreement through for the acquisition of the road. And when the party on the other side says that he has done his part, and we are not in a position to take strong ground that he has not, the most that can he said being that there is a doubt in the matter, surely the part of justice to the people of Canada, without injury to any one concerned, the part of common sense; and, above all, the part of a trustee doing his full duty,- is to take the measures and means at our hand to remove the cloud and place the people-inasmuch as they have decided that they will acquire the road-in a position to obtain a title not susceptible of attack even unfounded, attack based upon such difficulties as have been brought to our attention in this matter. I submit that the amendment which is moved is one that, if carried, can have only one possible effect, and that is to deprive the people of Canada of an additional security with regard to their title to that which they are about to acquire; and I cannot understand why amy persons in the Parliament of Canada should think it incumbent upon them to see to it that the Government do not make sure of a clear title in favour of the people.

speechtext: I did state that the Government had made a blunder in regard to that which we proposed to correct in the first section of the Act. I do not attach very much importance to that point, however, and shall not dwell upon it. But let me give my hon. friend a simple illustration. If I agree with a merchant for the purchase of a dozen barrels of flour, and I pay him or give him my notes, which is what the Government has done in this case,-

speechtext:
If I obligate myself for the dozen barrels, and be gives me ten and I go away satisfied, I think I have made a blunder. And that is what these gentlemen have done. They have accepted the ten barrels of flour, having agreed to pay for a dozen; and if they accuse the Grand Trunk of trying to mislead and deceive them, though the Grand Trunk may be in part responsible the Government are also responsible for their own mistake. If I go deliberately and take ten barrels of flour and pay for twelve, I can hardly blame any one for my blunder. But that is not the important point. In the argument of purchaser and vendor my hon. friend has made an amazing mistake, or rather I should say there is amazing weakness in his contention. In the ordinary relations between purchaser and vendor there is no Parliamentary power in question. The ordinary purchaser and the ordinary vendor will each do the best he can to protect himself, and will make the necessary arrangements to insure that he will be fairly treated. But my hon. friend forgets that the Parliament, of Canada in this matter is not a purchaser. We are called upon to exercise, not the ingenuity of a purchaser, but the power of a legislative body. We are called upon to exercise the supreme power of Parliament when we take away Lorn some one in England a right and privilege which , he thinks he has. There is no getting over that. Some people in England-erroneously, I am willing to believe, if my hon. friend says so,- allege that they have a grievance. They did not get proper notice, or' some right or other was not accorded them, and if they are to be suppressed it is by Act of Parliament and not by any action of an ordinary purchaser. We are in a sense a purchaser, but we are, in the higher sense, a Parliament; and if any man in England, connected even remotely with the Grand

Trunk Company, feels that he has been improperly treated owing to some defect in the proceedings in the meeting over there, it is not the business of this Parliament to turn him out of court. He should be left to the courts of the country to have his grievance settled. When my hon. friend applies the ordinary law of purchaser and vendor to the present case, he overlooks the fact that at this moment we are not acting as purchasers but are exercising our Parliamentary power, and undertaking to do that which the purchaser in ordinary transactions has no power to do.

speechtext:
I do not wish to detain the House unduly in connection with the discussion, either of the clause or of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne. You must have observed with pleasure, Mr. Chairman, the recent accession to the Government ranks. No doubt hon. members opposite were called in so that they might be ready to vote on a question the discussion of which they had but partly heard, in prder that the Government might be saved from such a defeat as was obviated the other evening by your casting vote. No doubt instructions were given to this end to the members supporting the ministry in this House. I do not propose to go over the debate which was held in the House on the question of the Grand Trunk acquisition last year. Wisdom is justified in its children, and I am glad to say that rarely in the history of this country has the Liberal party taken a stand in regard to which it was not justified before many years, or indeed months, had elapsed. The Liberal party took a stand last session against the acquisition of this railway on the terms proposed, and we have not had to wait very many months before that stand has been justified by the events that have occurred since. When we pointed out last session that a certain stock-I forget which, but I think it was the four per cent debenture stock-had^ risen by reason, of the expectation of the taking over of the railway by the Government, from the neighbourhood of between 40 and 50 to somewhere between 70 and 80, we were told it mattered little. We also pointed out that the Grand Trunk Railway in the last few years had spent money on dividends which should have been applied to railway betterments. But all in vain; the Government insisted upon the Bill going through as it was proposed. One of the great arguments made by the Government at that time was that 854
we must deal not only justly but generously with the British investor, the idea being that we were not only helping the British investor but that we were helping the Canadian borrower who in time to come, would be seeking capital overseas. I hold in my hand a report of the meeting-of a meeting -of the Grand Trunk shareholders held in London on the 19th February. It is reported in The Times of Friday, 20th February 1920. I think it is essential that these facts should be put before the people of this country so that they may understand fully how mistaken the Government were in thinking that they could conserve the credit or prestige of Canada in the minds of people who had made a loss by imposing what we denounced as an improper and improvident bargain u'pon the Canadian people. I read first from the remarks made by Mr. Reginald Woodworth: He said:
I have for the last three years voiced my feelings pretty strongly at the meetings of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I have felt- and I know something about Canada, for I have friends and relations living there who are engaged in financial and other operations-I have felt that we were going to be let down. At that time Sir Alfred. Smithers would not accept that view. Of course, being the head of this company, he could not accept it; but now he has acknowledged that I am right. I have seen that the Government would do, and was doing, all in its power to depreciate our property and buy us up at a breaking-up price. That is what is going to happen, and my reason for speaking to you is this. No one in this room feels more bitter, more disgusted, with the attitude adopted by the Canadian Government than I do myself.
Further on this gentleman proceeded to say:
The Government had absolutely made up its mind to get this company at a bankrupt price, (Cries of " Shame.'')
You will remember that in the debate which occurred on this matter last autumn the hon. member for Shelburne and'Queen's (Mr. Fielding) pointed out that there had been a rise of about $28,000,009 in the price quoted for certain shares of the Grand Trunk upon the stock exchange in London. Nevertheless these shareholders say that the Government was endeavouring to buy their property from them <it a bankrupt price. Another gentleman, Mr. Grant Hooper, said:
I am the holder of several thousand pounds of third preference stock, and I therefore take a keen interest in the company. I appreciate all that you have said to us to-day, and I feel that there is little more to be said, except that we should, as it were, dot the i's and cross the t's. I feel that a government is no more entitled to act dishonestly than an individual - (hear, hear)-and, whether it is the British

Government or the Canadian Government, I say that it should not act dishonestly.
Then he proposed that the following resolution should toe passed:
That this meeting, though accepting the agreement imposed upon the company, protests against the treatment to which it has been subjected by being refused permission to increase rates and in the limitation of the amount of the arbitration award.
But probably the gem of the whole meeting-and I believe this will interest members no matter whether they sit on this side of the (House or the other-was a .speech delivered by a reverend gentleman toy the name of the Rev. (Leonard Dawson. In mv experience I have generally found that when ministers of the gospel, or priests of any denomination, enter into mundane affairs they are generally as outspoken in their remarks as are the laity and this gentleman was no exception to the rule. Here are his words:	,
Rev. Leonard Dawson said that he was a considerable holder of the third preference and ordinary shares, and he had lived in Canada for a number of years. He thought they ought to look at the other side of the picture. The great trouble all along had been that this company was an English company. Their shares were not even quoted on the stock exchange in Canada and their board had been almost wholly an English board (a voice-quite right). They were dealing with-he put it quits frank-ly-a Canadian Government, which had no morals.
My admiration for this Government does not ooze out at the soles of my boots, Mr. Chairman,* but I would certainly be loath to say that in the private walks of life and in their personal personality-if that is not tantological-they were devoid of morals. It is true they sit before us as usurpers; it is true that they are responsible if not directly at least indirectly-because those who were not directly responsible joined with those who were-for the War-time Elections Act.
