speechtext:
In introducing this Bill the minister mentioned that he had two purposes in view: first, the correcting of these errors-this the minister said was the really substantial purpose of the Bill-and, second, that of ratifying the entire agreement. In the amendment which has just been voted down we on this side expressed our willingness to meet the Government in the matter of correcting the errors and of giving what was necessary in the way of ratification in that connection. The fact that the Government is not satisfied with what it proposes as the main purpose of this Bill leaves but one impression, and that is that in asking for ratification of the agreement as a whole there is some ulterior object which thus far has not appeared. When we are asked to ratify the entire agreement it is only proper that we on this side, before expressing our views one way or another upon it, should express our opinions in regard to any features of the agreement which we think should be made the subject of review before the final vote is taken.
In this House a day or two ago we had an important discussion on the manner in which certain of the employees of the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been treated by the company in regard to pensions to which they believed themselves to be entitled. As hon. members will recall, in the strike of 1910, which involved all the employees of the Grand Trunk Railway system, a settlement was effected whereby the employees were to be reinstated in their former positions. After the agreement had been adopted and the employees had returned to their duties, they found, much to their amazement, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company was unwilling to give them their rights in the matter of pensions.
In the agreement which we are being called' upon to ratify I find the following under the caption "Superannuation and Pension Funds," which is section 17 of the agreement :
The Grand Trunk Superannuation Fund shall continue in existence and shall continue to be administered as at present, and in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the same. The rules and regulations of the Grand

Trunk pension system shall continue to he applicable to employees of the Grand Trunk system until a general pension scheme applicable to all employees of Canadian Government owned or controlled railways shall be adopted and become effective. The rules and regulations ot the Grand Trunk Insurance and Provident Society shall continue to be applicable unless and until the Government shall adopt and make effective a general insurance scheme applicable to all employees of Canadian Government owned or controlled railways. In no case shall any acquired rights or vested interests in either the pension system or the Insurance and Provident Society be affected.
It will be perfectly apparent from this section of the agreement that the pension scheme of the Grand Trunk Bailway Company is an important feature of it. But the two sentences to which I wish to direct particular attention are the following:
The rules and regulations of the Grand Trunk pension system shall continue to be applicable to the employees of the Grand Trunk system until a general pension scheme applicable to all employees of Canadian Government owned or. controlled railways shall be adopted and become effective. ... In no case shall any acquired rights or vested interests in either the pension system or the Insurance and Provident Society be affected.
The employees of the Grand Trunk who were involved in that strike have been deprived of their rights in the matter of pensions. The company claim that that is in consequence of the employees having gone on strike. As was stated in the House the other day, there is no doubt from a reading of the agreement in settlement of the strike that the company was obliged to reinstate the employees in their former positions and that their status was to be what it formerly had been. Any one interpreting the language as the ordinary man would interpret it-certainly as the employees involved in the strike interpreted it-would be led to feel and would have good reason to believe that the employees should have all the rights which they would have had if they had not gone out on strike.
But, Sir, the discussion the other day brought forth a statement from the Minister of Justice which really has caused me to intervene at this stage of the discussion and to ask that before we ratify this agreement this Parliament take such action as will make it absolutely certain that employees of the Grand Trunk Bailway Company receive what is their due from the company. When this matter came up the other day it was pointed out that some legal technicality might prevent the employees from receiving their rights, and the attention of the Government was directed
fMr. Mackenzie 7Dng\]
to the distinction between what might be a legal right and what might be a moral obligation. I think I am correct in saying that the Minister of Justice said that the Government would impress upon the Board of Arbitrators just as strongly as they could the desirability of taking into account any claims which the employees of the Grand Trunk Bailway Company might feel that they had in respect of their claims to pensions. I understood him to say that if the Board of Arbitrators found there were legal reasons which would make it impossible for the board to regard the liability of the Grand Trunk these claims in respect to pensions, then there would be a moral obligation upon the Government when it became .sole owner of the road to rnakb good these pensions. What does that amount to? It means that the Government is prepared to say to the Board of Arbitrators:	If you cannot find that the employees are legally entitled to these pensions and that the Grand Trunk Bailway Company should be held liable for them, we will shift that liability over to the people of Canada. I say that that is a course which should not be permitted. The Grand Trunk Bailway Company of Canada owes the workingmen who were formerly in its employ every cent they should have received in accordance with the terms of the pension fund as it would have existed had there been no strike, and no technicality should be sanctioned by this Government or this Parliament which will permit the Grand' Trunk Bailway Company to escape their responsibility and the people of Canada to be mulcted in an additional payment of money which rightfully is a liability of the company My hon. friend, as a distinguished member of his profession, knows very well that the moment the Board of Arbitrators are asked to consider the question they will say at once that this is a matter of contract which must be dealt with in accordance with principles of law; and that there are in the provinces statutes of limitation which make it impossible to take cognizance of matters of contract after a certain number of years have elapsed. It was ten years ago that the strike took place, and I think that, in Ontario at any rate, after six years have elapsed no court can take' cognizance of any matter of this kind. Now, Sir, there is one court above all others in the land, and that is this court of Parliament, and I say that we at this time have it within our power to do justice to men who have had a great injustice done them for a period

of ten years. A great wrong has been done a large working class in this country, and I for one purpose to exert every bit of my-power as a member of Parliament to see that the wrong is righted.
I have different reason^ for feeling strongly on this matter. In the first place, my name has been introduced into the discussion in a manner which would lead the employees of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to believe that, because while a member of the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I intervened to help in bringing about a settlement of the strike, therefore in some way I was responsible, or at any rate the Government of Sir Wilfrid Lauiier was responsible, for the employees not receiving their pensions under the Grand Trunk Railway scheme. In the House the other afternoon a communication was read, which I shall read again in a moment, and which carries with it its own implication. It is a copy of a letfer which I sent to the leaders of the strike. The letter is dated, Ottawa, August 2, 1910, and reads:
Dear Sir:-Re dispute between Grand Trunk Railway Company and its employees in train anu yard service.
I beg to confirm over my own signature the following wire sent you at a quarter past five this afternoon:-
" Confidential-Mr. Hays has given Sir Frederick Borden and myself an undertaking that the men will within three months from this date, be taken back into service and within that time be placed in their former positions. We understand by the men all the men referred to in the agreement signed by both parties. In accordance with our understanding I shall expect to hear by wire immediately that the strike has been declared at an end. I will confirm this wire by letter over my own signature."
Tours faithfully,
W. L. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour.
S. N. Berry, Vice-Pres., O.R.C.
James Murdock, Vice-Pres., B. of R. T.,
Representative of the General Committee, Grand Trunk and Central Vermont,
Grand Union Hotel, Montreal.
Reference to the calendar of that time will show that the communication was sent on a Monday, and reference to the agreement as to the settlement of strike differences discloses that the agreement was dated 31st of July, 1910, which was a Saturday. Now, what was the agreement? I shall read it:
Agreement for settlement of differences dated 31st July, 1910.
Re dispute between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and its employees in train and yard
io-vice.
By way of settlement of existing difficulties:
1.	The company will put back as soon as possible the men other than those who have been or may be found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct, the understanding being that there is to be no coercion or intimidation towards the new men.
2.	The company will put into effect from May 1, 1910, the rates named in schedule of rates dated July 18, 1910, those rates to be embodied in the present schedule now in effect on this line, it being understood that those rates in no instance are a reduction in any existing rates.
3.	The company will, on January 1, 1912, make effective in train and yard service on the Grand Trunk Railway, the rates of pay and the rules contained in the schedule or agreement on that date in effect on the lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway east of Fort William.
The three above propositions shall apply also to the Central Vermont Railroad Company, the said railroad to be substituted for the Grand Trunk Railway, and the Rutland Railroad to be substituted for the Canadian Pacific Railway wherever the same are used or understood in the above. (In the case of the Central Vermont by the "schedule of rates dated July 18, 1910" is meant the schedule issued by the management of that company since July 1.)
Chas. M. Hays, President. Grand Trunk Railway System.
For the O.R.C.:	For the B. of R.T.:
John Maloney,
J. A. Connor,
W. C. Berry,
P. A. Hebert.
A. B. Garretson,
President, O.R.C.
W. G. Lee,
President, B. of R.T. Approved: S. N. Berry, V.P.
Approved : James Murdock, V.P.
Members of the committee will see that the agreement was drafted and signed on Saturday, the 31st of July; that my telegram stating that the men would be reinstated was sent on Monday, August 2nd; that the first clause of the agreement said that the men would be back "as soon as possible," while in my wire I stated that the undertaking was that they would be back "within three months" from that date.
As I explained to the House the other day when we were discussing this question in another connection, we had succeeded, in the course of the adjustment of the difference, in getting all questions in - dispute settled except the question of the time at which the men were to be taken back. The President of the Grand Trunk Railway Company desired to use in the agreement the words which appear there, "as soon as possible." He was unwilling to give any definite period of time; and Sir Frederick Borden, who was at the time Minister of Militia, and myself were in Montreal together and intervened between the company and the employees, helping to bring about
Robert Kelly, N. Foy,
Ed. L. Sinclair, .1. E. Munn.

the agreement between the parties. But what we did in particular that was of significance in the matter was that we insisted on Mr. Hays fixing a definite period instead of the term "as soon as possible," and the reason why the strike could not be settled on the Saturday was our inability to get any definite assurance from him as to precisely what he meant by these words.
Let me recall the circumstances that existed at that time so that the Government and the country will see the significance of the request I am making at the present time. The Grand Trunk Railway system was tied up from Chicago to Portland. The whole of the system in Canada was in such condition that practically not a train was running. I think that some of the passenger trains were kept up, but so far as freight service was concerned traffic was absolutely tied up. There were towns throughout the province of Ontario in which the people were in circumstances almost equal to those that might exist in a state of siege. They could get no food or commodities from other parts, and the whole country was suffering from the effect of the strike. Every day, almost every hour, meant millions of dollars of loss in different directions, and it was all-important that the strike should be brought to a conclusion as quickly as possible. As I have said, everything was settled on the Saturday except the meaning to be attached to the words "as soon as possible," and it was not until Monday that we were able to secure a definition of them, fixing the limitation of three months. It so happened that at the time the strike was on Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, was in the West. He had with him two or three of his colleagues, and at the moment the strike occurred I happened to be the only Minister of the Government in the city.
That being the case, and having had as Minister of Labour, some extra responsibility thrown on my shoulders in connection with industrial disputes, I took particular care to keep a record from day to day and, as I have mentioned, Sir Wilfrid Laurier being in the West, I took occasion to write him very fully that he might know exactly what had transpired in connection with the negotiations in so far as the Government was concerned. This evening I looked up some former files and I have here a copy of the letter which I sent to Sir Wilfrid Laurier at that time. It details the whole matter of the strike settlement, and I propose, with the permission of the committee, to place the contents of the letter on
[Mr. Mackenzie King !
record, inasmuch as they disclose exactly what took place in the meetings between the employees and the company, exactly what was the attitude of both parties, and exactly what is or should be expected as a result of the settlement. It bears strictly on this question of pensions, because this is a vital feature of the settlement. In the interest of the men, I am desirous of having laid before the Board of Arbitrators the fullest information it can possibly have. I am still more desirous that Parliament shall deal with this matter firmly before it Teaches the Board of Arbitrators, and that it shall deal with it so definitely in connection with this agreement that, so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned, there shall be no escape from its doing what it is in duty bound to do.
There is the reason I have mentioned why we should take this position, there is also the shameful attitude which the Grand Trunk railway has assumed towards its employees ever since that dispute took place. In order that I may bring this particular matter to the attention of the public, let me read this one communication to illustrate how arbitrarily, how unfairly, that company has dealt with its employees. Here is a communication, which speaks for itself, from a conductor of the Grand Trunk railway:
Mr. C. Forrester,
Superintendent.
Dear Sir,-I was notified yesterday that I was to be taken out of service on account of not being able to pass eye examination before Inspector Kloyhill, and take the opportunity of making application for pension, as I notice by clause No. Si and 10 in Book of Rules and Regulations of Pension Fund that I am entitled to it, that is if I understand the rules. I have been in continuous service for the company for nearly forty years, and during that time have been in charge of some of the heavy way freight trains, and have been very successful so far as I know in handling same; also think I should have a consideration for length of service, as I am getting well up in years and do not feel able to go out and battle the world over again. Am sixty years of age, and if you can possibly do anything for me along this line would look upon it as a favour.
Hoping to hear from you in respect to this matter, I am
Tours truly,
A. Pennington.
This is the reply which he received:
Stratford, Ont., March 1,9, 1914 Mr. A. Pennington,
(Palmerston, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of March It in regard to putting you on Pension Fund. Did you .participate in the Trainmen's strike of 1910? If so, I regret to say that you cannot

participate in the benefits of the pension. The fact that you voluntarily left the service at that time and was out of service for two weeks debars you from that privilege, from the fact that any one participating in the pension must claim continuous service, while those who left the service on account of that strike have a broken service.
-	Yours truly,
C. Forrester, Superintendent.
I need not go any further to give the reply made by Mr. Pennington to Mr. Forrester, but what I wish to point out is that the company deliberately construed the circumstance that the men had taken part in the strike as a ground for not permitting them to have the benefits of the pension fund, even though, as in this case, some had suffered bodily injury while working on behalf of the company and had served for forty years. The whole understanding on which the men returned to work, and returned to work in the public interest, as members of this House will appreciate when they hear the correspondence, was that they should be put back in the positions which they had held before. I say that that sort of treatment is unjust and unfair, that it is affecting thousands of men and their families in this country, and that it is the duty of Parliament to act where it sees so great an injustice affecting not only this class of employees but also having a direct bearing upon all the relations between employers and employees as well as a bearing upon the attitude of the Government towards labour, and when it is of such wide and far-reaching significance in relation to the whole industrial problem of our times, to intervene and see that justice is done.
There is a further reason. Not only do the Grand Trunk Company take shelter behind the language of the statute governing the pension fund but they would have the employees of the Grand Trunk believe that because this Parliament gave them that charter they cannot do anything for the employees on the ground that it would be contrary to an Act of Parliament. I want to make it perfectly clear to the Grand Trunk Railway Company that this Parliament is prepared to give them every right and to see that the statute is construed in a broad and generous way and in accordance with the spirit of the settlement. If the Grand Trunk is taking refuge behind any subterfuge and, as hon. gentleman must know, from what I have just read here, they are, we must take care to see that before this matter is disposed of all doubt shall be removed. My hon. friend says that the Government would be ready to assume
this obligation if the Arbitration Board were to pass it on to the Government and not make the Grand Trunk liable. How can my hon. friend say this Government will have anything to do with the Grand Trunk railway at any time from now on? The Government has not such a strong hold upon life that it can ftope to live very much longer, and before the arbitration is concluded we may see the Government out of office. The Government has not the support of the people of the country.

I think they would be much safer than they are at the present time, but my hon. friend cannot speak even for hfs successors. He can only speak for himself. I want to put this matter beyond any peradventure, and to insist that this question shall be settled and settled satisfactorily. There is a time and a place for everything. We have come now to the last moment 'in which justice can be done to these men. It can be done by the action of this Parliament while we are dealing with this agreement. To put it off is to open the door to doubt to keep these men in a condition of uncertainty and to keep open this great grievance. Now is the time to close it up as speedily as we can.
Here is a communication which the Grand Trunk has sent to two or three members of the railroad brotherhood:
Montreal, April 8. 1914.
Mr. Sam'l Pugh,
Chairman O.R.C.,
Montreal, Que.
Mr. John Maloney,
Chairman B. of R.T.,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dears Sir:-Replying to your communication of February 2nd.
Under the Rules and Regulations for the establishment and administration of the Grand Trunk Pension Fund in accordance with the powers conferred upon the company by the Act of the Dominion Parliament passed in the year 1907, continuous service for a sufficient period is necessary to entitle an employee to ask that his application for pension be given favourable consideration.
The Rules and Regulations have been formally approved by the directors of this company in accordance with the requirements of the Act, and the committee is not at liberty to depart from or vary them.
Therefore the employees to whom you refer must again qualify by continuous service for a sufficient period from the date when they returned to the service of the company to again become eligible to participate in the privileges under the Pension Fund.
Yours truly,
Howard G. Kelley,
Vice-President.

There, Mr. Chairman, is a distinct statement-

speechtext:
Montreal,
April the 8th, 1914. *There is a distinct statement to the effect that the Parliament of Canada has in some way bound the Grand Trunk Railway Company so that it cannot fulfil the obligations which it is morally-and, I believe, in any true meaning of the word legal, legally bound as well to carry out. I say there is a technicality which they have thus far taken advantage of; and we have no right, in the interest of the working people of this country, in the interest of industrial peace in this country, and in the interest of justice, fair play, and decent treatment, to let this agreement go through and have this thing remain unsettled.
Now, Sir, there is a further reason, and that is that the working men belonging to the different brotherhoods have themselves appealed to the Government to see that justice be done to them in this matter. I share the surprise of an hon. member of this House who, when we were discussing the matter the other day, said he wondered how the Government, when they were drafting this agreement with the Grand TrunkRailway Company, or when they were bringing forward a Bill to give them power to make the agreement, gave no consideration whatever to the representations which had been made by labour. In this connection let me read the representations which the Government had before them at the time the Bill was brought into Parliament at a previous session. There was a meeting of the railroad conductors of America and Canada, held in May, 1919, and a resolution of the Canadian delegates was adopted and forwarded to the Government. Let me read the resolution in full, because it gives' the strongest reasons why, at this time, we should see that this matter is finally and equitably settled:'
Moved by N. Roy, No. 75, seconded by P. Hill, No. 624.
That we, the accredited delegates, representing all railway points in the Dominion, to the 36th session of the Grand Division of the Order of Railway Conductors of America and Canada, resolve as follows, that:-
Whereas in 1907, the Canadian Parliament enacted 6-7 Edward VII, Chap. 89, An Act respecting the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, empowering the Grand Trunk Railway Company to establish the Pension Fund from its earnings for the beneiit of employees retired from the service on account of old age; and,

Whereas we believe Parliament, though it did not so provide in the Act, surely intended that the said Pension Fund would be administered by the Pension Department of the Railways fairly and without discrimination ; and,
Whereas the said company, through its Pension Department has debarred its employees from the benefits of the said Pension Fund be-"cause they participated in a strike of the Conductors, Brakemen, and Yardmen, on the road in 1910, and,
Whereas, it is well known that the said strike was the result of the unreasonable attitude assumed by its then management, in refusing to grant the employees increased wages and improved working conditions based on the standard wage and conditions on other Canadian railways, and,
Whereas, it is well known that the transportation brotherhoods, including the Order of Railway Conductors, do not strike until all other means of settlement have been exhausted, and.
Whereas, the employees who participated in the strike of 1910 had the sympathy of the citizens generally and especially those citizens located along the said railway, and,
Whereas, the Government then in power affected a settlement, and it was agreed among other things that the employees would return to work and resume their standing in the service and their seniority rights held by them prior to the strike, as though they had been continuously in the service, and,
Whereas, the company has since the said agreement deprived the said employees who have retired from the service on account of the age limit from the benefits of the Pension Fund, alleging that their participation in the strike in 1910, broke their continuity of service with the company, and,
Whereas, many conductors and other train men that had served the company and the public faithfully and continuously up to fifty-three (53) years, and having reached the age limit have been retired from the service, and for the reason above stated debarred from, the pension which they so sorely need on account of the low wages in effect on this road prior to the strike of 1910, and,
Whereas, the accredited representatives of the Order of Railway Conductors and Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen having appealed to the management of the Grand Trunk Railway, and also to its Board of Directors domiciled in England, and its Chairman, Mr. Smithers, for the restoration of the said pensions without success, and in pursuance of the policy of these organizations to exhaust all legitimate efforts to reach a peaceful adjustment of all matters affecting the interests of their membership, therefore be it
Resolved;- that we respectfully petition the Government and Parliament of Canada-
Notice those words. I am reading at the moment a petition from a large body of the workingmen of this country, not only to the Government but to the Parliament of Canada, and I am asking Parliament to hear that peititon.
to use their good offices to the end that the Grand Trunk Railway Company's Pension Department shall recede from its unjust attitude, and that in future it shall administer the Pension Fund of that company fairly and without
f

discrimination, and tljat it shall pay to its employees all arrears of pension due them, and, Whereas, we are advised that our Government is desirous of acquiring the Grand Trunk railway and incorporating it as part of our National Railway system, and is negotiating to that end, therefore, be it further,
Resolved, that we respectfully petition our Government not to conclude said negotiations for the purchase of the said Grand Trunk railway without providing for the protection of the pension interests of the employees concerned, and he it further,
Resolved, that we furnish a copy of these resolutions to the Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, and to the following ministers of departments, and members of Parliament, namely:-The Honourable Minister of Railways, J. D. Reid; the Hon. Minister of Labour, G. D. Robertson, and J. E. Armstrong, Esq., M.P., Chairman of the Railway Committee of the House of Commons.
A. D. Fidi.er,	.
Division No. 463, Calgary, Alta., *Chairman, Caucus,
Canadian Delegates.
A. S. Emms,
Division No. 611, Kamloops, B.C., Secretary.
W. V. Hurdon,
Division No. 286, Fort William, Ont. Mr. Chairman, there is a request from the employees of the Grand Trunk Railway system to the Government and to this Parliament that before this matter is concluded, justice be done to them. I repeat again, this is the only time, as far as I can see, when there is still an opportunity to heed that request. The Government thus far have ignored it altogether; they have paid no attention whatever to the demands of the Grand Trunk Railway employees in regard to this pension fund. They have talked fair to them in one way; they have done nothing in the way of action. They have repeated again the other day in the Rouse what they have said to different deputations: "We will urge this;" "we will urge that,"-knowing full well all the time that all their urging does not amount to a snap of the finger. I say, Mr. Chairman, that is no way for a government tol/deal with railway employees. That is the kind of treatment that these men have had to put up with from the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and if the Government themselves have ignored their express wishes in this regard, I, for one, demand that this Parliament hear them. Let me make my position as emphatic as it is possible to make it on this subject. We can now settle th.is question in a satisfactory way. All we have to do is to add to this agreement an amendment, which I shall propose as soon as I have concluded what I have to say, and ihe full rights of these employees will be finally determined and justice done.
Vow' Sir, I -must ask the committee to pardon me if the communication which I am about to read is a somewhat lengthy one but I think hon. gentlemen will find it extremely interesting. I am sure it will be it revelation, not only to the employees of the company-some of whom have been led to believe that others than those who were really blameable were responsible for their not receiving the pension-and I think it will prove a little enlightening to the people cf this country. What I want to have the committee keep in mind as I read this communication is, that when these matters were under negotiation the whole of this country was tied up as a consequence of that strike, and that the attitude of the men and the attitude of the company was every hour affecting the interests of every citizen of this Dominion. The attitude of the Grand Trunk Railway Company was arbitrary and inconsiderate-I cannot use words too strong to express the feelings that I had toward the company in their behaviour at that time.
The action of the men was manly, considerate, with due regard for the interests of the people of this country. Had the action of the men been otherwise, with the action of the company what it was, Heaven alone knows what might have happened in Canada at that time. Our people as a whole are indebted to the working men on the Grand Trunk Railway system for the attitude which they then maintained, and they are indebted to an extent which they will never be able to repay. Low the chance comes to see that these thousands of men and their families who have been deprived of pensions shall have justice done to them. It is up to this Parliament to see that justice is done.
Well, Mr. Chairman, as I said Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in the West and I wa3 part of the time alone in Ottawa-it was in the summer. Mr. Smithers, the president of the company, was, I think, about to go to the West, and as I was anxious that Sir Wilfrid should have full knowledge of the facts so that they could be placed before the president, I wrote very fully, well realizing that a strike of such great proportions would in all probability be of significance for some years to come, and knowing the men I had been dealing with, that out of it there might develop just what has since happened. My letter is dated August 4,1910.1 shall not read the first few pages, which deal with conditions that existed prior to and led up to the strike, but I shall read from the point at which I refer to the intervention of the Gov-

ernment in the matter of settlement of the strike, and that naturally begins with what I cannot avoid as a reference to myself in my duties as Minister of Labour at the time. I wrote:
I was the only minister in the city during one or two days after the strike commenced, and the Immigration Department referred its messages respecting procedure as to strikebreakers, etc., and the Justice Department a telegram as to troops, to me. I took the ground that the law and regulations as laid down should be carried out with strict impartiality, and that no exception to any provision should be made in favour of one side or the other, that neither as to train service or military protection was any department of the Government to take any course other than that which it could justify on the basis of existing legislation. If requests came for troops through civic authorities in accordance with the provisions of the Militia Act well and good, the provisions of the Act should then be followed, otherwise the Dominion was to give no military protection. As to immigration, no exceptions were to be made to meet an emergency one way or other. This course Mr. Blake Robertson, of the Immigration Department, in the absence of Mr. Scott, carried out to my mind in a most efficient manner, so much so. that with the possible exception of the company, the public and all others interested are, I think, prepared to commend his action. Had he wavered, it is difficult to say what serious trouble might not have resulted.
My course in the department was to carefully size uo the situation on the first day. see the extent to which the public were being embarrassed and then to bring about arbitration through force of public opinion, if that were possible. To this end. as you know, I addressed an open communication to each of the parties, and received evasive answers from each. I addressed second communications, insisting on a direct reply, and received an answer no less evasive from the company and one partially evasive from the men. The last named communication indicated a restricted authority, so I communicated again, with a view of getting an answer from a final source. This answer came on Saturday, the 24th, accepting arbitration as offered by the Government, and was immediately communicated to Mr. Hays. Mr. Hays gave no reply until ten o'clock Sunday night, at which hour he answered that the time for arbitration was passed. On Monday I wrote him, expressing the hope that as the one side were agreeable to arbitration, he might come later to express a willingness to do the same, provided this should appear to be in the public interest. All of these communications you have. Their effect, as a consequence of the attitude of the parties which they helped to reveal, was to draw public sympathy away from the company, with which it was pretty strongly at the outset, and to swing it with the men; so much so, that in almost every city and town of the province the boards of trade and the mayors of the several municipalities began passing resolutions and deluging the company with demands to refer the differences to arbitration. The voice of practically the whole press, Liberal and Conservative alike, became one in the same demand, while business concerns whose interests were suffering, and such organizations as wholesale grocers, the retail grocers. Canners* Association and the like, addressed resolutions

in unmistakable terms to the company. Not only was the demand the same, but the position also.-the Government of the country had called upon the two parties to arbitrate, the Government represented the people,-one of the parties had responded and it was the business of the other to do the same.
Had Mr. Hays really desired arbitration he had reason enough, if ever man had reason, to grant it at that time. The value of the company's securities were daily depreciating in England and abroad; the company's system was paralyzed; its losses occasioned through the crippling of its business was mounting up to the million dollar mark and over; whilst its additional expenses in seeking to man the trains with strike-breakers and re-commenee opera-aions in the midst of a struggle were only adding to the burden. From the financial point of view it was to the company's interests to settle; the people of the country wanted the strike ended, and the Government wanted it ended, but to all this pressure, and to public opinion in general, Mr. Hays remained wholly indifferent. This was the situation on Monday and Tuesday, a condition which intensified during the whole week.	[DOT]
On Tuesday we had a meeting of Council, at which I outlined what had taken place, and suggested that Sir Richard, as Acting Premier, should send some communication to Mr. Hays from the Government as a whole, this communication to be confidential. As the company was issuing statements from time to time to the effect that it was rapidly resuming operations on its lines, Sir Richard thought it would be well before taking a further step to get definite information on this source. Accordingly, we arranged with McDougald, of the Customs Department, to send a wire to the Collector of Customs in each town and city in the province, requested a wired reply, stating briefly the extent to which the strike was affecting business. Practically without exception the answers came in on the following morning from all parts of the province to the effect that on the whole of the Grand Trunk system not a freight car had moved in or out of the several towns from the time the strike had commenced up to the time of wiring. But what was worse than that, factories and mills were cldsing down in many places because raw materials could not be brought in or finished products sent out. It was also mentioned that shippers were being advised that the Grand Trunk could do nothing for some time. The C.P.R. and the other railways, where they were paralleling the Grand Trunk, had their facilities overtaxed and were not proving equal to the extra work put upon them. Customs receipts had fallen off considerably.
With this information before Council, on the following morning it was decided that a letter should be sent to Mr. Hays, and as Sir Frederick Borden was leaving the same evening for Nova Scotia, it was agreed that Sir Frederick would take the communication with him and see Mr. Hays personally, impressing upon him the seriousness of the situation from the point of view of both the Government and the country. I attach a copy of the letter, signed by Sir Richard, which, with some 40 enclosures, was the one taken by Sir Frederick to Mr. Hays.
Whilst we did what we could to bring pressure to bear on Mr. Hays in this direction, I had a feeling that a first-hand contact with the situation would prove ultimately the only means of dealing with it effectively. I did not like,

on top of the communications I had been sending to the parties to rush in without a request, though I felt that if Mr. Hays did not yield to arbitration on the strength of the letter from the Cabinet, the public were strongly enough at my back to permit of my going down to Montreal and sizing up the situation with a view of giving the public a clear-cut statement as to who was in the right and who was in the wrong. To strengthen my position as much as possible I arranged by letting them know of my willingness to do so, to have a communication sent me by the men asking my personal intervention. Sir Frederick left on the six o'clock train on Wednesday. At midnight on the same day a message came from the leader of the men in the following words:
" May I be permitted on behalf of the men on strike to request that as a minister of the Crown and representative of the people you come to Montreal and by further effort try and arrange an honourable settlement either by arbitration or negotiation."
As Sir Frederick Borden had taken a communication to Mr. Hays I requested the men over the long distance telephone to keep their communication to me confidential. I was fearful lest knowing I had been requested to come by the men, it might embarrass Sir Frederick in his endeavours with Mr. Hays. I promised I would go down but asked that nothing should be said as to why I was going or at whose instance. I got into communication with Sir Frederick and asked him to wait over a day with me, hoping that Sir Frederick with Mr. Hays and I with the men, we might together assist negotiations to the extent of getting a settlement.
I left Ottawa on Thursday afternoon. Sir Frederick met me at the Windsor station, and we dined quietly together. Sir Frederick said he had found Mr. Hays very pleasant, and that we would have little difficulty in arranging a settlement. He had arranged for our meeting Mr. Hays together at his house later in the evening, and at ten o'clock we drove to Mr. Hay's residence and had a talk with him and Mr. Fitzhugh on his verandah from ten until after midnight. In the course of this conversation the whole situation was carefully reviewed, the respective positions of the parties fully gone into and explained, and we left on the understanding that Mr. Hays was quite ready for a settlement to be negotiated, if Sir Frederick Borden and I could succeed in bringing it about.
I left Sir Frederick .at the Windsor shortly after half past twelve and myself drove on to the Grand Union Hotel, the headquarters of the Canadian leaders. I had had my secretary inform them earlier in the evening that I was having a talk with Mr. Hays and would be along and see them when it was concluded. 1 found them waiting and we had a conversation of an hour or two. It was agreed that they were to come to my room at the hotel on the following morning and we would consider what propositions it would be possible to submit to Mr. Hays. In the meantime, as Mr. Hays had expressed the opinion that no final settlement could be made without the presidents of the two orders, who happened to be in Toronto, it was arranged that they should be sent for, so that they could be on hand for final negotiations. This was the point we had reached by three o'clock Friday morning.
Friday, July 29 :	At ten o'clock on Friday [DOT]
morning the full committee of the men assembled in my room at the hotel. The whole situation was carefully gone over, and I was given authority to say to Mr. Hays that in the event of his agreeing to reinstate all the men, excepting those who had been guilty of violations of law or destruction of the company's property, the men were prepared to accept any of the following alternatives:-
(a) To leave all matters in dispute to arbitration, or (b) to accept the award of the Board of Conciliation and Investigation in toto, and where there might be any doubt as to the meaning of a particular clause to leave it to the chairman of the board to say what the meaning was.
Since the board's award had not been fixed the date at which the standardization of rates was to become effective, the men were prepared to either:-
(a) leave the question of the fixing of the date open for future negotiation; or (b) leave this question to arbitration and abide by the result; or (c) to consider arranging some satisfactory basis of settlement of this date by negotiation.
I was authorized to say that on the acceptance of any of these alternatives, with the understanding that what was accepted in th.3 case of the Grand Trunk would also be accepted in the case of the Central Vermont, which is considered a part of the company's system, the men were prepared to return to work immediately; or if Mr. Hays preferred to have the difficulties settled by negotiation in the first instance and before the strike was declared at an end they were ready to commence negotiations at once.
During the afternoon I called) on Mr. Hays at his office and had a long talk with himself, Mr. Fitzhugh and Mr. Biggar. Mr. Hays did not express either approval or disapproval of any of the alternatives, but asked me if I would leave him a copy of them. I did so on the understanding that it was not to be considered an offer from the men to him, but rather a proposal from myself to each of the parties as being the basis on which I believed a settlement could be immediately effected. His unwillingness to give any immediate decision was put down to the circumstance that Mr. Gar-retson, the President of the Order of Railroad Conductors, and Mr. Lee, President of the Order of Railroad Trainmen, would have to pass on any decision which was ultimately come to, and he thought it would therefore be better that proposals should come with their sanction before he gave them final consideration. I told him that Messrs. Garretson and Lee had been sent for, and asked if I might arrange for a meeting between himself and them to consider the several propositions. He agreed to this, it being understood that I would meet with Mr. Garretson and Lee and the committee again on the following Saturday morning, see him later, let him know what they were prepared to do and that a joint conference would then take place in the Board Rooms of the Grand Trunk Railway on Saturday afternoon. This concluded the first day's negotiations, and Sir Frederick, at my request, very generously remained over to be present on Saturday along with myself during the course of negotiations.
Saturday, July 30:	On Saturday morning
Messrs. Garretson and Lee, who had come in the interval from Toronto, together with other members of the committee, called at my room at 9.30. They endorsed the stand taken by the

Canadian members of the committee and authorized me to lay before Mr. Hays as from the men the several alternatives suggested on the day previous and to say that the acceptance of any one of them would be agreeable as a basis of settlement. After this interview, I asked Sir Frederick to come with me to Mr. Hays' office. We were met by Mr. Hays, Mr. Fitz-hugh, Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright. Mr. Hays began discussing with me the alternative proposals of the men, raising many objections. His endeavour during this interview was to have me commit myself on the different points but I was careful not to do so, though I did not hesitate to give him frankly my opinion as to the merits of any points he might raise.
As to the reinstatement of the men, he professed from the obtset to be willing to take them all back, with the exception of a few who might have been disorderly. Sir Frederick and I both took the stand as-*we were working now for a settlement in the public interest, that it was just as well that bygones should be bygones, and no discrimination made, except in the cases mentioned, because of men having gone out on strike. We had not been discussing very long before it became quite apparent that it was not a way out, but objections, that the company was seeking to raise. I took the position that I was not there to argue for one side or the other, but to assist the two to come together, and failing that to let the public know the reason why they were unable to do so. Mr. Hays seemed anxious that I should return with a counter-proposition to the men, and keep on going back and forth between them. I felt instinctively that his motive in this was not genuine, but that it was, if possible, to draw me into a position where he would find some means of escape by claiming that I had failed in making clear some understanding, or had misrepresented some situation, and I therefore demurred a little to this request, pointing out that I had already told the men that in accordance with the arrangement reached the day previous that they would be asked to come to a joint conference in the afternoon, and had got them to make the offer of the alternatives which I was presenting on that understanding.
We got our first true light on the situation when the question of the Central Vermont was raised. I pointed out that as all was considered part of the one system and the men had gone out simultaneously on both roads, they were standing together for a settlement of both at the same time. Mr. Fitzhugh thereupon broke into the conversation and said that when the Grand Trunk dispute had been before the Board of Conciliation in Toronto, the Chairman, Mr. Atkinson, had refused to consider the Central Vermont in connection with it. I said if this were so I would take the position that we, as members of the Government, were not concerned with the Central Vermont. I then turned to Mr. Fitzhugh and asked if he would be willing to leave it to Mr. Atkinson to say just whether the Central Vermont had been included or not. Mr. Fitzhugh replied: "No, I would not." After this reply' of Mr. Fitzhugh I appealed to Mr. Hays, Mr. Biggar, Mr. Wainwright and Sir Frederick as to whether they believed it was possible for any progress to be made with negotiations if we were to deal with each other in that fashion. I felt considerably annoyed, and could not help showing it, whereupon Mr. Biggar began to apologize for Mr. Fitzhugh, and say I could not have understood his meaning. Mr. Fitzhugh added that he had not intended to say anything offensive, that I must have mls-

understood him. I replied that I hoped this was so, and to prevent any misunderstanding I would repeat the questions. I then asked him if I were right in understanding that he had said that at the time the Grand Trunk dispute was before the Board in Toronto, Mr. Atkinson, the Chairman, had refused to consider the Central Vermont in connection with it. To this he replied, yes, that I was quite right. I then said that in the event of that being so, Sir Frederick and I would take the position that the attitude taken by Mr. Atkinson should bind us also. (I did not know at the time of speaking what attitude Mr. Atkinson had taken). I then said: "Assuming that this point should be controverted, would you, Mr. Fitzhugh, after having said that Mr. Atkinson ruled out the Central Vermont, be willing to leave it to Mr. Atkinson to say what he had done provided that we agree to follow his course and abide by his decision?" To this Mr. Fitzhugh replied that he did not think he should be asked to answer this question. I mention this instance because it is only one of a very large number, of which both Sir Frederick and I could tell you, of a not disimilar kind. From this on through the whole negotiations it seemed absolutely impossible to hold either Mr. Fitzhugh or Mr. Hays to any statements that they made. After Mr. Fitzhugh had taken the position he did, I said to Mr. Hays that it did not seem to me any good purpose could be served by our attempting negotiations, and was about to withdraw when Mr. Hays suggested we should all go to lunch. He invited Sir Frederick and myself, but we explained that it would hardly do for us to accept his invitation, and we went to the Windsor together. Mr. Biggar followed us to the elevator trying to apologize for Mr. Fitzhugh. I toldl Mr. Biggar he might tell Mr. Fitzhugh that he should remember he was speaking to responsible ministers of the Crown, that he must be responsible for the words he used, that I had hardly expected to see him put his company in the position he had, and that if the Central Vermont were to be the stumbling block in the settlement negotiations because of the stand he had taken, I for my part, would take good care to see that the public were fully informed of the cause.
When Sir Frederick and I returned after lunch, Mr. Hays and the other gentlemen were in the Board Room. I had Sir Frederick see Mr. Hays before I went up an explained to him that there was no use to try any bluff on me one way or the other, that I was there to do a piece of work and meant to see that it was done to the satisfaction of the public, that I would go any length in assisting him to get a settle-men which would be satisfactory to him, and be as considerate of fys position in the eyes of the public as possible, but that in this matter there was a big public duty to be discharged and it would have to be regarded in that light. When I came to the [DOT] Board Room, Mr. Hays took the position that I should go and see the men and take counter-propositions from him, that we should carry the negotiations over Sunday and perhaps reach a settlement during the coming week. I took the position that this strike was seriously affecting the public and that every hour was important, that it was not my business or purpose to act as an intermediary except in a way that was likely to secure results, that as the two parties would have to come face to face at some time in the proceedings they might as well do so at once. Sir Frederick also intimated that he was desirous of leaving on the following morning, and that

it would be quite impossible for him to stay over longer. By holding firm to this position Mr. Hays finally agreed that we should send for the men. The committee was on hand within half an hour. Negotiations then commenced between Mr. Hays and Messrs. Gar-retson and Lee, and we were favoured with about as interesting an afternoon's discussion as I think either of us has ever been privileged to listen to. Sir Frederick had gone down to Montreal with feelings very strong against the men. He told me that he had seldom been more impressed by the closeness and fairness in reasoning than he had been in listening to Messrs. Garretson and Lee. In every argument, he said, the men had the better of the company.
At the joint conference Mr. Hays submitted amendments in reply to the proposals which the men had made. They were base, so far as the rates of pay were concerned, on the award of the board, but left out altogether the question of rules, and the men made it apparent that any settlement would have to include rules at some time, though they were prepared to consider what time this part, of the award should go into effect. To make a long story short, we had. by half-past seven on Saturday night, reduced all the points at difference down to three simple propositions, the first relating to the putting back of the men "as soon as'possible" ; the second to the conditions to become effective at the present time and the third as to the date at which the standardization of rules as well as rates was to go into effect. In consideration of Mr. Hays moving the standardization of rates from January 1, 1913, the date he gave out at the time of the strike as that at which he would put into effect the standardization of rates, to January 1, 1912, the men agreed to forego the standardization of rules, (the main point in which was the payment on a mileage instead of on a per diem or monthly basis) from the present time, as awarded in the board's report, until the date at which the rates of pay were also to be standardized. Then, instead of accepting the rates of pay as set forth in the award of the board at present the men agreed to accept the rates as given out by Mr. Hays since the strike commenced, provided that in no case these rates were to be made lower than the rates existing prior to the strike. Everything, in other words, was settled, except the meaning of the words "as soon as possible." The men held out for an immediate reinstatement. Mr. Hays held out for reinstatement "as soon as possible" without giving any definitness to these words, though professing openly that he meant by them to take all men back, and practically all almost immediately. Mr. Hays refused to yield an inch on this ground, and told the men they might do as they pleased, that was as far as he would go. He then left the room with the other officers of the company. I asked the men to remain with Sir Frederick and myself. "When we were alone I said to them that I would like to speak very plainly, that I thought they had made a mistake in not agreeing to arbitration at the very outset, that in this they had not been true to the principles which their brotherhoods had always professed, that I was willing to grant that there might have been grounds for doubt as to the bona tides of any offer, but it was their business to have accepted it and to have looked to the Government to see that it was made good ; that as they had struck without arbitrating Mr. Hays had been forced to take on some 86
men to fill their places, it was only reasonable that they should allow him some time to get rid of strike-breakers he had employed, and to maintain the position which the business community generally would expect him to maintain ; that the words "as soon as possible" saved him in the eyes of the public, on the other hand, it was only reasonable that he should give these words some definiteness of meaning to all of us present. Having anticipated this very difficulty at the start, I had taken care when with the Canadian Committee at the first interview, to thresh out this point with them, and I got from one of the leaders in his own handwriting a statement which he thought would cover the ground, the men having met me at that time by agreeing to the use of the words "as soon as possible" provided it could be understood that they did not mean a time longer than thirty days.
