speechtext:
Thirty days in this case. This was the preliminary statement handed to me by one of the leaders. They were agreeable to thirty days; afterwards we had to change it to ninety days.
This statement I took out of my pocket and showed to Messrs. Garretson and Lee. I mentioned that in speaking to Mr. Hays I had felt justified in virtue of it. in saying that I thought thirty days should be allowed him to get rid of men who had been taken on as strike-breakers, that he knew I was committed to this extent and that under the circumstances I thought they could waive immediate reinstatement and allow thirty days. At once they said they would be wholly agreeable to this, that if Mr. Hays would give his word to Sir Frederick and myself that by "as soon as possible" he meant not longer than thirty days, the strike might be declared at an end on the basis of settlement which had been reached up to that time.
When we got back to the company's offices at nine o'clock I saw Mr. Hays personally and tried to persuade him in the interests of all concerned, to allow the first clause to go on the thirty days understanding, pointing out that as president of a company where such vast interests were concerned it would not do for him to let the wish of subordinate officials govern in a matter of this kind. It was perfectly clear in my own mind that a longer period was desired by some men only for the purpose of carrying out threats they had made that if the men once went out some of them would never get back again. He asked me to come in and talk over this phase with Mr. Fitzhugh, Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright. This Sir Frederick and I did, each of us strongly taking the position that a settlement should be reached on this understanding. We left him for a short time and he then came up to the Board Room with his other officers. The different points were gone over pro and con. We were agreed on everything except the words "as soon as possible," Mr. Hays repeating this over again, that we had got down now to a point where only three words "soon as possible" were keeping us apart. The men conceded the thirty days to meet him on this. He went over each statement carefully, saying that he wanted to make sure that he had them quite correct, and then left the room, as we all supposed, to draft a final agreement. He came back with a let-



ter addressed to Messrs. Garretson and Lee containing three propositions, at the end of which he had written, "We understand that the foregoing propositions are practically what you have accepted, with the exception of No. 1, which you think should be in the following form." He then set out the clause the men had suggested as to reinstatement and added that if they insisted upon their form of dealing with that portion of the difficulty he would agree to arbitrate as to which form of No. 1 should be adopted, his or theirs, the Board of Arbitration to consist of one arbitrator named by each of the parties and the third nominated by the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec.
When we examined the letter Mr. Hays had written it turned out that not a single one of the propositions was what we had all understood had been the position reached. Instead of May 1 being mentioned as the date at which, new rates of wages were to come into effect, July 18 was fixed as the date. It had been agreed that C.P.R. rules as well as rates were to go into effect from January 1912, but his new draft did not mention C.P.R. rules, but made reference to rules in the award, with a clause that they might be subject to modifications to be mutually agreed on between the company and committees representing the men. These changes which completely altered the whole agreement as it had been come to ten-atively were pointed out to Mr. Hays. He admitted one mistake after the other, saying that clearly there was an error. Notwithstanding that every one felt more or less shocked or exasperated, we got over this difficulty and back again to where we were before he took the proposals down-stairs. There was left then only the first clause and the three words.
Sir Frederick by this time had become pretty well tired of Mr. Hays' methods of negotiating and began himself to put one or two questions to Mr. Hays, asking him to name some time- any time-a year or more, as long as it was definite, within which he would agree to take back the men, but he could get no answer from him one way or the other. The men said as to arbitrating between the two propositions they were willing to leave them to either Sir Frederick or myself to say what was a reasonable time, that they would not bind us to thirty days, but leave us to name any period we thought suitable, but this Mr. Hays would hot agree to. Finally, after some pretty sharp words between Mr. Hays and the men and some very pointed questions from Sir Frederick, Mr. Hays got up in a very excited condition and went away, telling us we could do what we liked. Before he left, the men turned to him and said, "Mr. Hays^ if you are unwilling to complete a settlement with us at the present time, here is out last proposition: It is to leave this whole matter to a board of Arbitration, the arbitrators to be named, not by ourselves or by you, but by either Sir Frederick Borden, Mackenzie King, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy or Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We will take any board named by any one of these gentlemen, and we will leave it to you to say which one you wish to name the board, or we will agree to a Board of Arbitrators chosen in any other way that is fair."
You may know what a pass matters had come to when both Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wain-wright came to Sir Frederick and myself and begged of us not to judge him too hastily. I then got hold of the men and asked them not

to declare negotiations at an end; the following day was Sunday and to let us have one more try on the next day. Their reply was "Mr. King, we were through, but as you have asked us, we wish to close no door, we will wait just as long as you say." It was now after midnight, and Mr. Biggar, Sir Frederick, Mr. Wainwright and myself drove up to the Mount Royal Club where we talked the situation over for another hour and a half. Both Mr. Wainwright and Mr. Biggar offered to help us all they could. It was agreed before we left that they should see Mr. Hays in the morning and we should see him in the afternoon and see if we could not come a little closer together.
Sunday, July 31.-It was nearly three when Sir Frederick and I turned in Sunday morning. We breakfasted together after a sort of night's rest and after breakfast I drew up in the form of an agreement what he and I, listening to the negotiations, believed and knew to be the several propositions tenatively agreed to. W6 decided that we would lay this proposed agreement before each of the parties and give them each a chance to sign. In this way we could test the bona tides of each beyond question. Moreover, in order that Mr. Hays should be afforded no reasonable excuse for hesitating to make an immediate settlement, we decided that we would place as interpretation of the words "as soon as possible" a period not exceeding three months, instead of thirty days, as giving ample time to reinstate all the men, and also affording some measure of punishment to those who may have been offenders in mild ways. Mr. Wainwright and Mr. Biggar came to our rooms about noon, and wTe read over to them the terms of this proposed agreement They agreed with us that the several propositions it contained were those tenatively agreed to by the parties on the night previous, and they thought they should prove acceptable to Mr. Hays. It was then arranged that they would see him before three and that we would meet him about half past three.
In accordance with this arrangement we arrived at Mr. Hay's house at half past three. He invited us into his billiard room with Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright. They had arranged to keep Mr. Fitzhugh away, so as not to embarrass the situation. We opened out by mentioning that we had all been tired the night before and that in this state of mind things had become a little confused, and that to clear matters up we had written out what we thought had been the points reached by the two parties. I had had about ten of these statements prepared, it being my intention to have copies ready to hand around should there be several of us considering them at the same time. I went over each proposition and each was agreed to in turn by Mr. Hays. WTien we had concluded the document we were all agreed that it contained the tenative arrangement, and that if we could find a satisfactory solution of the words "as soon as possible" the strike would be ended. Sir Frederick and I then said that we thought instead of thirty days, if three months were named, that ought to meet the situation. It would give ample time to find places for men at present employed. Mr. Wainwright and even Mr. Hays also agreed that there would probably be only a very few that the company would wish to keep. When we thought Mr. Hays was about to sign he suddenly turned to us and said, "Well gentlemen, where do you come in on this? I give my note for three months, it falls due and the

obligation is wholly upon me; where do you come in?" Sir Frederick replied that we became the endorsers. We had a little laugh over this and thought Mr. Hays was only joking, but he went on to speak of different things, what hard luck the road had had in different directions, of the need of reduction of coal duties, of increased allowance for carriage of mails, etc., etc. We told him that of course we could not speak for the Cabinet, that we were only two members, but that we would certainly be only too pleased to represent to our colleagues anything he might do to help out the present situation. We thought they would not be lacking in good-will toward him for anything he might do. He then said he thought if we wanted him to take back any of the men we should agree to take any men who had been taken on since the strike and whom he might not be able to find positions for or get rid of at the end of the three months. He said he supposed work could be found for them on the I.C.R. or if not on the I.C.R. provision might be made in some other way.
I happened to know that all of the men who have been taken on have been engaged by the month, and that he is under no real obligation to them, and I felt that he was only bluffing for some reason of his own, and when Sir Frederick asked me what 1 thought of it, I said that it seemed to me very reasonable that Mr. Hays should make such a request, that in fact it showed his good faith in the promise he was giving to reinstate all of the men. We were asking him to take back every one; he said he had obligations to some whom he had taken on since the strike commenced ; we therefore, I thought, should be prepared to meet him at this point, provided the obligation were not likely to be serious, as he himself had stated. Sir Frederick said he held the same view, and then used words to this effect: "Now let us see what is the extent of the obligation we are assuming; we agree that if there are any men who have been taken on since the strike and whom Mr. Hays may have still in his employ at the end of three months and is unable to find positions for, the Government should relieve him to the extent of undertaking to find some suitable employment, either on some of the railways in the Dominion or in some other way." After Sir Frederick and I had each carefully stated our obligation and asked if this were right, and it was so admitted by Mr. Hays, he said, very well, that he would sign the agreement on that understanding. He then took the nine or ten copies of the agreement which I had drawn up, went to another room and returned with all of them duly signed.
He had said before leaving that I could, perhaps, when I got back to the hotel or later on, send him a little memo of the obligation on each side. I had felt instinctively that there was something to be watched in this, and therefore decided to write out the memo on the spot, and while Mr. Hays was away signing I drafted out what we had understood was the nature of the obligation. The draft which 1 then prepared and which I read over in an unfinished form to all present was as follows; (Of.course it was understood that any arrangement made in this connection was to be entirely confidential, as was also the interpretation to be put on the words "as soon as possible" so far as the public was concerned. Sir Frederick and I were only to give our word to the men that Mr. Hays had given this assurance to us) :
86J
By the way, may I say here in parenthesis, lest it should appear that I am communicating any matter which it was decided at the time should be confidential, that I repeated over and over again to Mr. Hays, during the negotiations, that one of the reasons why I desired him to settle was that there would be no necessity for making public the extraordinary record which I am giving to this House at the present moment. I told him that if, when a settlement was made, he did not carry it out he might expect the whole transaction from beginning to end to be made public.
"Re settlement of dispute between G.T.R. Company and employees in train and yard service.
"Confidential.
"Dear Mr. Hays:
As hon. members will remember there were none of these men in the employ of the company at the end of three months because the strike breakers were employed only for a month, and we knew at the time we were negotiating that there would be no obligation towards any of them because the strike would be over. We were not taking on any liability for the Government but we simply included this in the draft.
"With regard to the agreement signed by yourself to-day as a means of settling existing differences and our conversation in reference thereto, we understand that you undertake to reinstate within three months in their former positions in the company's service, all of the men involved in the present strike. We have your statement that since the strike commenced you have taken on a number of new men, any of whom still in your employ three months hence you will be under obligation, to provide for. It is apparent to us that the present strike cannot be terminated unless you give the above undertaking. We realise that its continuance even for a day, to say nothing of an indefinite period, will mean heavy financial, not to speak of other forms of loss to individuals in all parts of the Dominion, as well as serious injury to industrial and. commercial conditions in Canada and without his knowledge we feel we would fail in our obligation to the people of Canada, whose trustees we are in this matter if we allowed the possibility of your being unable to provide for all such employees to prevent a settlement. We therefore undertake, in order to prevent such a contingency, that the Government of Canada at the end of three months will relieve you of such obligation as you may still have in this respect, by providing in a fair and equitable manner for any men who have joined the Company's service since the strike commenced and who may be still in your employ and for whom you are unable to make further provision, etc., etc."
When I had read over this draft Mr. Hays said he did not like the word "reinstate" and I asked him what he would suggest instead, and he said "take back." I said very well, it would read then, "undertake to take back' in their former positions in the Company's service."
/

viz., the restoration of full service on the Grand Trunk Railway with every consideration possible to the men who went out on strike, and while we are not entirely in accord with you in the meaning you attach to the clauses quoted, where room exists for a different opinion, there should be no difficulty in arriving at some mutually satisfactory settlement, should occasion make necessary, and with this understanding your proposition is accepted.
"Tours truly,
"Chas. M. Hats,
"President."
When shown this letter, I gave the one obvious reply, that it meant nothing, and if accepted by Sir Frederick Borden and myself as giving the assurance required would only lay us open to having taken as an assurance what was not such in fact. Thereupon Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright explained that Mr. Hays had nothing of the kind in mind, that as a matter of fact he had arranged that if this letter were not satisfactory and left any room for doubt, Biggar, Wainwright and myself were to come to some understanding as to the interpretation to be put upon its words,-the understanding to be embodied in the memorandum to be attached to the letter, this memorandum to be signed by Mr. Hays and myself. I said immediately a satisfactory memorandum could be drawn up that would be wholly agreeable and we began to discuss its terms. Mr. Biggar presented me with a typewritten memorandum which he thought would meet the case. The memorandum as presented was anything but satisfactory. The first clause read as follows:
"The men shall within three months from this date, be taken back into service and within that time be placed in their former positions. This, however, is not to require the removal from any of such positions, of men who were in the company's service prior to the strike ; the intention being that those formerly occupying such positions shall get them back from time to time as vacancies occur."
I pointed out that the second sentence of this paragraph nullified the first; that unless all of the positions spoken of in the second sentence became vacant before end of three months it would become impossible to carry out the undertaking in the first sentence, which was the essence of the whole situation. Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright admitted this and struck out the second sentence. They then' asked me whether I thought the Government would undertake to look after the men who had been taken on the company's lines west of Detroit, between Detroit and Chicago, and east of Montreal, between Montreal and Portland. I replied that we could hardly be expected to do that, that I thought that by undertaking to look after such men as might be left in the Company's employ in Canada, we were going about as far as it would be possible for the Government to go. They were also of that opinion, and having drafted a memorandum on these lines, they took what wa's acceptable to me, and what I think they believed to he fair and in accordance with Sir Frederick's undertaking and my own, to Mr. Hays. They were absent about an hour, and then came back with a memorandum, the first sentence of which, instead of reading-
"The men will, within three months from this date, be taken back into service and within that tin" he placed In their former positions-'>. read-

"The men formerly in the company's train and yard service in Canada will within three months from this date be taken back into service and within that time be placed in their former positions."
I saw at once that here again was a new device to enable Mr. Hays to carry out one of only two possible intentions in his mind, either to have no settlement at all, or to settle only on the basis of not taking back all the men, which he knew very well was the only basis on which a settlement could be reached, except by a strike which might last for several months. I pointed this out to Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright. They replied that they did not think such was in Mr. Hays' mind, that he had said, if we were limiting our obligation to Canada, he should limit his obligation to Canada also, and that for this reason he felt the memorandum was absolutely fair. Besides he did not see why as Canadian Ministers, we were concerned with the Tankee end of the situation.
Knowing that Mr. Hays had been unwilling to negotiate a settlement until Messrs. Garretson and Lee as presidents of the organizations were on hand, in order that whatever was come to might be binding on all; knowing too, that the question of who were included in the word "men" or "all men" had never once been raised in the whole discussion, either with me privately or in negotiations with the men or in anything that occurred during the time that Sir Frederick was present; knowing that the one and only pretext up to that time had been the difficulty of finding an interpretation to the words "as soon as possible" which related to time and not to nationality; knowing further that by a deliberately false manceuvre this ground had been shifted by Mr. Hays away from the question of time to the class of men to be cared for by the Government (i.e. those of the strikers who might fail of reinstatement instead of those of the men engaged since the strike who might still be in the Company's employ at the end of three months) ; knowing that in the letter sent to Sir Frederick Borden and myself in reply, another evasion of the whole question had been sought, with the deliberate intention to have the Government shoulder responsibilities which might place It before the whole labour world as having Intrigued with a corporation to gain a certain and,-I could not help feeling how fraught with truth were the words that "patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel."
I left Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright and returned to the hotel. They thought I had gone to see how this proposition would appeal to the men, they had said Mr. Hays wished me to put it to the men, and if they would not accept it, that would he their own lookout. Sir Frederick and I as Ministers would have done our duty, and the Canadian public would be well satisfied at our having taken the stand which we had taken, and that public opinion would strongly back Mr. Hays in his patriotic endeavours.
When I reached my room I drafted two letters, one to Messrs. Murdock and Berry the Canadian leaders. It was a draft based on the assumption that I could get from Mr. Hays all that had been asked in reference to Canada, and concluded with the request that they would advise me whether or not this would be acceptable to the men whom they represented. The other letter was a letter to Mr. Hays in reply to his letter to Sir Frederick and myself, briefly mentioning that there should be little difficulty in our arriving at an under-

standing as to what was meant by the words on which he placed a different interpretation than our own and ending with- a request that he inform me wherein his interpretation differed from ours. I called the committee to my room and read over to them the draft letter which I had addressed to Messrs. Berry and Murdock. I said that I was not submitting that letter to them, that I had not received from Mr. Hays the undertaking therein expressed, but that I would like to know whether if such an undertaking could be received and were such a letter sent by me to them, would the strike be ended. They replied that I knew as well as they did that it would not, that for them as Canadians to agree for themselves alone to what had been gained for them through their fellow workers all over the system would be to play the part of traitors to their fellowmen. My answer to them was that as Canadians I would be mistaken in them if I thought they would take any other stand, and that as men I would be ashamed of them. I asked them, however, if they saw into what position the whole strike would be brought if such a communication should be sent and an answer demanded from them. I pointed out that they could not blame Sir Frederick and myself if Mr. Hays put this proposition up to us, as I was afraid he might do, and demanded of us to pass it along; that we should then be obliged to write a communication such as I had written to them. They admitted this was so. I told them that was all I wanted; it was not my intention to allow them to be put in this position before the public of Canada. On the other hand, I was anxious that they should know just how far the Government of Canada was standing by them in an endeavour to see fair play and to get justice in the present situation. They replied to me: "Mr. King, whatever you do, whatever you ask, or whatever you say, we will approve of your course."
I then returned to Mr. Wainwright's office. When he got hold of Mr. Biggar they asked me how the men had taken the proposition. I replied to them that I had made no proposition to the men, that so far as the men were concerned I was through with them; I had their signatures to a document on a certain understanding which they were prepared to stand by; that I had no reason to doubt their faith in the obligation they had assumed, and that the only thing which was now preventing a settlement and which had prevented a settlement from Saturday night up to that time, was to my mind the mala fides of Mr. Hays ; that I was prepared to be still undeceived as to this, but' I hoped they remembered, and as advisers of Mr. Hays would see that he thoroughly understood, that every step in the endeavour to find the light in this situation might some day be publicly disclosed. I then asked if I was right in understanding the letter given me. in the morning over Mr. Hays' signature as replying to Sir Frederick's and my own, and was informed, "yes." I then drew from my pocket the following letter, and said, "Give this to Mr. Hays as my further reply to him:
"Montreal, August 1, 1910.
"Dear Sir: -I have your letter of to-day acknowledging the receipt of the letter of July 31 from Sir Frederick Borden and myself, and note that you say that you are not entirely in accord with Sir Frederick and myself as to the meaning we attached to the clauses quoted. AVe have given you the meaning and the only
meaning it has seemed possible for us to place upon the clause in question. However, if room exists for a different opinion, I agree that there should be no difficulty in arriving at some mutually satisfactory settlement. Perhaps you will kindly inform me wherein the meaning you attach to the clause quoted is not in accord with Sir Frederick's and mine, or what is the meaning you attach to this clause.
"Yours faithfully,
"W. L. Mackenzie King,
"Minister of Labour." "Chas. M. Hays, Esq.,
"President, Grand Trunk Railway System,
"Montreal."
When Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright received this letter they were in a state of consternation. They each admitted frankly to me that Mr. Hays was a man that nothing could be done with, and they saw no possibility of a termination of the strike. We spent an hour talking over the position, trying, the three of us together, to find some means that could end the difficulty. Before leaving I turned to Mr. Biggar and Mr. Wainwright, and said: "I see only one faint glimmer of hope which can save all. It means more in the way of responsibility than I can take on my own shoulders, but perhaps my colleagues, knowing the situation, will help to carry it with me. to save this country and to save Mr. Hays." They asked me what it was. I asked Mr. Biggar if the reason Mr. Hays had given for refusing to include all men in his undertaking was because I had limited the Government's obligation to the men in Canada. He replied: "Yes." I said: " Do you think that if the Government were to extend its obligation to include all, Mr. Hays would extend his also." Mr. Biggar replied that if he did not there would be no ground left for him to stand upon. Then I said: "Very well, Mr. Biggar, you can give this letter to Mr. Hays, and you can say to him at the same time that if that is his reason, if he is prepared to sign the understanding we have reached on the ground that ' the men' means exactly what it says in the one paragraph as well as the other, I will be prepared to ask my colleagues to give me authority to sign the memorandum on the basis of this understanding, but before I ask them to do this Mr. Hays must have expressed his readiness to sign without reservation, mental or otherwise. I will then know, as you will know, that that alone, knowing the man we are dealing with, can terminate this strike and save all the direful consequences which must follow from either its continuance or a disclosure of what has transpired is an effort to negotiate a settlement." Biggar and AVainwright looked more than relieved. They agreed that the obligation could mean little or nothing, and virtually admitted that it was simply a pretext; after it was understood that Mr. Biggar would spend the morning with Mr. Hays and secure, if possible, his signature, and that Mr. AVainwright would come to Ottawa and be present to sign there on behalf of Mr. Hays with his authority, after Mr. Hays had signed in Montreal himself, and take back the document with my signature if it could be obtained. I left them and returned by the 10.30 train to Ottawa, getting in at 1.30 a.m.
Tuesday, August 2-This was the position when 1 was again at my office on Tuesday morning. X inquired what ministers were in the city, and found that Mr. Brodeur and Dr.

Pugsley were the only ones present. Mr. Wain-wright arrived at noon. He had not yet heard from Mr. Biggar, hut said he expected to do so any moment. We agreed that we should meet at the club. Mr. Brodeur joined me at luncheon, and when we came out of the dining room we met Mr. Wainwright, and I asked him if he had received word from Biggar. He said he had; that all was now satisfactorily arranged, if the Government could see its way to enlarge its part of the undertaking. Mr. Biggar had, while we were talking together, suggested the words " men on the Grand Trunk system," as the best words to include in the document, it being understood that the Central Vermont might have to be considered as part of the system if Mr. Hays so suggested. Mr. Biggar, however, did not intend to raise the point with him. Wainwright said: " In the phone message which 1 have received Biggar tells me that Fitzhugh has insisted with Mr. Hays on having the clause read 'The Grand Trunk Railway or Central Vermont."' "The Central Vermont," he said, " is Fitzhugh." I then told Mr. Wainwright that Dr. Pugsley and Mr. Brodeur were the only other ministers in the city. I had expected from a wire Sir Richard had sent me from Kingston that we would be having a meeting of the Cabinet (but Sir Richard had been unable to come). On hearing this Wainwright said that Mr. Hays had signed the undertaking as submitted to him by Mr. Biggar, and that he (Wainwright) had been authorized to say that on my signing, either alone or with the consent of other ministers, that would be enough, and that he was authorized to sign at this end on Mr. Hays' behalf the similar document we had here. I then asked Mr. Wainwright if he would meet Dr. Pugsley, Mr. Brodeur and myself at three o'clock. Mr. Brodeur and I talked over the whole situation, and we all met in Dr. Pugsley's office at three o'clock. I then went over the whole story with Dr. Pugsley and Mr. Brodeur in Mr. Wainwright's presence, very much as I have narrated it in this letter, so that they were familiar with all that had taken place. I asked Mr. Wainwright in their presence if he were quite certain that they were agreed to sign this undertaking in the form in which we had finally drafted it; this would end the strike. He said: " Yes." I asked him if we did not, did he know of anything else that would save the situation. He was still more emphatic in saying that he did not; that he felt this was absolutely the only thing that could be done to, on the one hand, terminate the strike, and on the other avoid an open rupture between the Government and Mr. Hays and the disclosure of all that had taken place. Wainwright said that he doubted if all of the men that would be left on the system, including the Central Vermont, would amount to more than a few dozen at the outside, if. as a matter of fact, there were any at all. All the men who had been engaged had been hired only by the month, and there were few of them who were really any good. Besides, the company would be opening up new parts of lines, and would be needing extra men before the next three months were completed. He did not think the whole thing would really amount to anything. I asked him if he were quite positive there could be no further hitch. He said: "Quite." Also, he said to Dr. Pugsley and Mr, Brodeur: " I am ready to sign on the authorization of Mr. Hays, who has already signed, and if my authority to do so should be ever questioned by him, I am prepared to hand in my resignation as vice-president of the company." [Mr. Mackenzie King.)
It was perfectly evident to my mind that there could be no estimating the seriousness of the situation that might arise were the public on the morrow to be informed that despite all that had taken place in the way of negotiation there was only a prolonged dispute to be expected on the road. I had been given to understand by the men that the engineers and firemen were going to quit unless a settlement were reached,

not out of sympathy, but on the ground that the trains not being properly manned they felt it too hazardous to continue their runs. With this prospect before us, and knowing the man with whom we were dealing, I felt it was our duty to sign, and so expressed myself. Dr. Pugsley and Mr. Brodeur were of the same opinion, and we three then signed the memorandum, and Mr. Wainwright signed as follows: " Authority of President, by William Wainwright, second vice-president, Grand Trunk Railway system."
I then returned to my office and sent a confidential wire to Messrs. Murdock and Berry, the Canadian leaders, stating that Mr. Hays had given to Sir Frederick Borden and myself an undertaking that the men would within three months be taken back into the service and within that time placed in their former positions, and that in accordance with our understanding I would expect to hear from them by wire immediately that the strike had been declared at an end. Within half an hour I received this word. About this time Mr. Biggar phoned me from Montreal to know how negotiar tions were proceeding. I told him what had transpired and that the strike was off. I then wrote Mr. Hays, saying that having received from him the undertaking asked for in our letter of July 31, Sir Frederick and I were able to assure him, not only that the strike would be immediately terminated, but that it had been declared at an end. I then mailed to each of the parties under registered cover, copies of the agreement by which each were bound. I wired you, mentioning that the strike had been concluded through Government intervention, and after wiring Sir Frederick gave out to the press copies of the agreement without comment, other than that the agreement spoke for itself. Before the night was over, I am informed, every man from Chicago to Portland over the whole system had reported himself as ready for duty.
This letter, I fear, is already much too long, but it has seemed to me owing to yourself and the Government that all of the important circumstances should be fully narrated and carefully recorded before there is possibility of any future misunderstanding.
And then there is one paragraph-I am omitting some others here-which shows our position on this matter and which shows to what extent the interests of the men were really protected and safeguarded at that tjme.
There is one other thing:
This is still part of my letter to Sir Wilfrid.
I see by the press that Mr. Hays Is proposing to consider as cancelled all obligation which his company may be under in the way of pensions, partially or all but fully earned by any of the men who may have gone out on strike. A pension has always been considered a reward

of servicTe,-not a. manacle to fetter personal liberty. Some of the men who have been out on this strike have, I understand given thirty-four years of their life to the company's service. They, according to Mr. Hays, are to lose every cent of their pensions, and start in as new men. Unless Mr. Hays or those who control his company, are prepared to recede from this position, my own individual view is that the Parliament of Canada would be justified in refusing to grant any company with which Mr. Hays is concerned any further consideration of any kind, and that the Government should lead Parliament in this view. If, as Mr. Hays will probably say, he cannot legally grant the pension, Parliament might help to rid him of this limitation by enacting legislation which will give him the legal power he requires. It is to be hoped for the sake of the interests of the company, to say nothing of the rights of others, that his directors will not allow him to persist in a stand of this kind.

speechtext:
' I know my hon. friends opposite are anxious to get through with this matter in a hurry; but this has been standing for ten years, and if it is going to take all night to-night and all day to-morrow to obtain justice for these men, I am prepared to stand here in order to obtain it. For ten years I have stood in this country under fire of hon. gentlemen opposite as one who betrayed the workingmen in this particular situation, When I was not in this Parliament where I could raise my voice, some hon. gentlemen opposite were out on platform after platform throughout this country pointing to me as the cause why these men had not received their pensions. I have waited until to-day to tell the whole story; I am going to tell it all, and I am not through yet.
Mr. MeMASTER:	It will be best to be
patient.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
There is something eternal about justice, and if it is going to be possible to prove the truth in this case on behalf of the workingmen of this country, that is going to be done. In that letter to Sir Wilfrid Laurier I stated all the facts at the time and it will be apparent to any hon. member that such a letter could only have been written immediately after a situation of that kind. I went into the matter in great detail, because I was fully conscious of the tremendous responsibility I had to assume as a single individual at that time when the Prime Minister and other ministers were out in the West. The Minister of Railways was also away, and I was, therefore, careful promptly to put in every detail. Had the Grand Trunk Railway Company carried out its obligations, not a line of this would have been made public. Had the
Grand Trunk Railway Company reinstated the men, not a line of this would have been made public. Had the Grand Trunk Railway Company, within the past ten years, been willing to do what was honest and fair and straight and just with these men as regards pensions, not a line of this would have been made public. But making this public ought to be the means of compelling this Parliament, before it proceeds further with this agreement, to see that this opportunity does not pass without full justice being done to the men in this matter. I think I have made it perfectly clear to the House that if it had not been for the patience and loyalty of thSse employees of the Grand Trunk Railway Company ; if it had not been for their willingness to do all in their power to bring this situation to an end, no one can tell into what disastrous condition this country would have come, because the situation was a most critical one. The men having acted in that way, it is up to Parliament to see that no further jockeying is done with regard to their rights.
I concluded my letter to Sir Wilfrid Laurier by stating that until the Grand Trunk Railway Company came to their senses in the matter, until their president acted in an honourable way, no further assistance should be given by the Government to that company. There is seated beside me this evening the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) who was Minister of Finance in Sir Wilfrid's Government at that time. He can bear out the truth of what I say, when I tell the committee, as I do, that at the time this matter was under negotiation, Mr. Hays had been coming to the Government for assistance in connection with some of his lines in the West; he had asked for a very liberal amount, as is the custom, and the Government was favourably disposed to help him. What was the answer that Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave him? Put back those men into their positions and carry out your agreement, and I will go before Parliament and get you your money. Mr. Hays said that he would, but he never did. Another week passed and then another, and we dissolved Parliament without Mr. Hays getting a five-cent piece, although it was millions of dollars that he was after at that time. What was our reason for taking that position? We took the position that until the company was honourable in regard to its obligations and carried them out, the company would not get another five-cent piece from Parliament if we could avoid giving it to them. That statement haa

never before been made public; but the former Minister of Finance will recall that that was the position taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in dealing with this company, and the reason that the Grand Trunk Railway Company did not receive any assistance from the Government of Canada, until another Government took office, was because the company did not carry out those obligations. The Minister of Labour knows well enough the trouble he had of bringing Mr. Hays later on into line in getting anything done. What I want to make clear is this. If we are to have a contest between any corporation and the Government of Canada, are we going to let the corporation have the last word, or are we going to insist upon the Government of Canada having the final say in a matter of justice? I want to say to the Government that that is the situation to-day. This has been a long battle; it has been a fight as between a great railway corporation and the Government of Canada as to who is to have the last word in a matter of justice and honour, and my hon. friends opposite cannot afford to allow this opportunity to pass without seeing that this matter is put once and for all where there will be no chance of escape on the part of the Grand Railway Company from meeting its liabilities to the fullest possible extent.
I have taken up a great deal of the time of the committee, but I feel that this is a matter than which there is nothing of greater importance to this country at the present time. What is the greatest question that we have before us? It is the question of industrial relations. What is the proper solution of it? It is straight and honest dealing and nothing more. If you have not confidence you get nowhere in the industrial world or in the improvement of industrial relations. Parliament is the custodian of public honour. The Minister of Railways, if he examines the reports of the debates which took place at the time this matter was under discussion, will see where he himself, pointing to me, said over and over again: The Government intervened in this matter; they should get justice for the men. Now my hon. friend has the chance. He can put in this little agreement an amendment which I am about to move, and that will adjust the matter for all time.

speechtext:
I repeat that
to the extent of millions of dollars the Grand Trunk was refused assistance which it asked for at that time. I recall very clearly that they came for this assistance within a couple of weeks of the dissolution of Parliament. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in England attending the coronation. My hoh. friend (Mr. Fielding) was Acting Prime Minister at the time, I think; I know that he had in hand the legislation that the Grand Trunk was asking for. It was held up during all the time that Sir Wilfrid was in England. It would- have been introduced while he was abroad if the men had been put back to work. The Government notified Mr. Hays that as soon as the men were reinstated the legislation would be introduced. Sir Wilfrid returned, and I think he had been back only about two weeks when Parliament dissolved. I myself heard Sir Wilfrid say to Mr. Hays: "I will keep Parliament in session two weeks longer to give you a chance to put these men back and to have full justice done to them. I will then bring in the legislation that you want. But I will not ask Parliament to vote a cent to the Grand Trunk Railway Company until these men are reinstated." That course wras never taken. Parliament dissolved, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company never got their money.

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had taken the position that no further legislation would go through in the interests of the Grand Trunk until they had settled with these men, that would have been all right. But I make the statement that the then Minister of Labour at that session assisted in putting through legislation for the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I take issue
with my hon. friend; the record will speak for itself. The strike took place in July, 1910. The matter of the three months' reinstatement came to be a question at issue

while the session was on. I think it was the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) who pointed out the other day that the question whether any of the men had been guilty of the violation of law had been referred by mutual consent to Judge Barron. It was well on in 1910 or in the beginning of 1911 before it was known what men were to be reinstated, but once it became apparent that the Grand Trunk was refusing to reinstate, certain of the men, we refused to introduce a single bit of legislation on behalf of the company. Every hon. member on this side who was in the House at that time knows that very well. The records will bear out literally every word that I have said.
Now, Mr. Chairman, 1 move that section 2 of the Bill be amended by adding as subsection 2 thereof the following words:
The said agreement is hereby amended by adding thereto under the caption "Superannuation and Pension Funds" the following:
"Any right or interest of any employee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company existing in either the pension system or the Insurance or Provident Society prior to the strike of the company's employees which occurred in July, 1910, is hereby declared not to have been affected by the said strike or any circumstance or condition arising out of or in connection therewith."
Let me just say a word in conclusion. There is not a line in that amendment which is not in full accord with what was understood at that time by Sir Frederick Borden and myself, who represented the Government of Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that as members of the Government it was up to us to see that that obligation was fully discharged. I have pointed out to-night, in language which, I think, is unmistakeable, how difficult it was at the time the strike was on to get justice done. I have also shown wherein every effort was made while the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in office to have that wrong righted. The member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) who was my successor as Minister of Labour, worked hard-every one on his side knows how hard he worked -to get justice done in the matter of the reinstatement of the men. He tried also to effect adjustment in the matter of pensions, but was unsuccessful, and that matter has not yet been settled. If this chance goes by there may be no possibility of settlement for a long time to come. All that the Government have promised is that they will urge upon the board of arbitration the consideration of the moral or legal obligation. But the Government know that so far as
the legal obligation is concerned the board will probably take issue with them upon the ground of the bearing of the statute of limitations upon matters of contract.
The Government have intimated that if the board makes a finding along another line the Government will be under a moral obligation to make good these pensions. That is shifting the liability from the Grand Trunk Railway Company to the Government, and that should not be permitted. This is a debt owing by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to certain of its employees. It is a liability, if there ever was a liability upon a company, which ought to be met by the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself and not transferred to the people of Canada . So I ask that we take advantage of this opportunity to put the matter beyond peradventure and to save the honour of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the honour of the Government and the honour of this Parliament by seeing that justice is done where justice has been long overdue.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the risk of detaining members of the committee for a few moments at this hour of the morning, I desire to say a few words in reply to the speech delivered by the leader of the Opposition (Mt. Mackenzie King).
I have been much gratified at the enthusiasm which my hon. friend has manifested to-night in championing the cause of those of the Grand Trunk employees who struck in 1910, so far as pensions are concerned. I regret that he did not manifest that enthusiasm earlier. It is now nearly ten years since the agreement was effected to which my hon. friend has referred. That agreement provided, in substance, that all men who had been on strike, except those Who had been guilty of any violation of the law, should be reinstated within three months and that they should be paid an increase of wages dating back from the first of May, 1910. Although my hon. friend assisted in the negotiations to bring about this agreement there is no reference to pensions in it. He was in power from July, when that agreement was entered into, until a year after the following October, a period of fifteen months. He states that about three months after the agreement was entered into it was ascertained who were entitled to be reinstated. There were about two hundred men whom the company refused to reinstate. A judge was appointed to go into all these

cases, and he reported that 138 of these men were entitled to be reinstated under the agreement that was made in July, 1910. Now what has occurred? You heard my hon. friend say tonight, Mr. Chairman,-I was surprised at the statement, and I hope some explanation of it is forthcoming-that the Government of which he was a member constantly refused to do anything for the Grand Trunk Railway Company until they should discharge the full duty of reinstating these men, and giving them their rights respecting pensions.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext:
The statement made
by the hon. gentleman was that no legislation would be passed by the Government of which he was a member. I have here the statutes of 1911, and the House will remember that the agreement was entered into in July, 1910. The particular statute in question is not of great length and I had better read it. It is under date, April 4, 1911, nearly eight months after the agreement was signed:
Whereas a petition has been presented praying that it be enacted as hereinafter set forth, and it is expedient to grant the prayer of the said petition:' Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows :
1.	This Act may be cited as the Grand Trunk Act, 1911.
2.	The expression, "the company," where used in this Act, means the Grand Trunk Railway .Company of Canada.
3.	Notwithstanding anything iri the Railway Act heretofore passed respecting the company,
[Mr. Crothers.l
any of the various classes of stock heretofore or hereafter authorized to be created and issued by the company shall be transferable ini such manner and upon such conditions as shall be provided by the by-laws of the Board of Directors of the company.
4.	The company may acquire, hold, guarantee, pledge, sell or otherwise dispose of shares of the capital stock, bonds, debentures or any other securities heretofore or hereafter issued by the Montreal and Southern Counties Railway Company, and for that purpose may utilize any funds of the company, including proceeds arising from the sale of any class of stock which the company is now or may hereafter be authorized to create or issue, and upon the acquisition of any such stock, bonds, debentures or other securities, may exercise all the powers thereof and receive any dividend or interest paid thereon.
5.	The company may guarantee, upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon, the due payment, as the same matures, of interest at the rate of four per cent per annum upon first mortgage bonds to be duly issued by the Grand Trunk Western Railway Company, for a principal amount not exceeding $30,000,000 payable fifty years from the date thereof: Provided that to the extent necessary the proceeds of such bonds shall be utilized in the payment or redemption of any outstanding bonds and any overdue coupon appertaining thereto issued by the said Grand Trunk Western Railway Company, and guaranteed by the company, under or pursuant to the provisions of the Grand Trunk Railway Act, 1901, or of the agreement sot forth in the schedules of the said Act.
(2) Nothing in the preceding subsectioij shall be regarded or construed as in any way limiting, curtailing, or impairing any of the powers now vested in the company.	-
I shall not read the other sections, but I may quote the short titles. They are as follows:
6.	Power to issue perpetual consolidated debenture stock. 7. Ranking and conditions. 8. Application of proceeds of stock. 9. 1888, c. 58, s. 6 to apply. 10. Commencement of Act

Certificate of chairman-.-copies of certificate-legal evidence.
During the same session, under date May 19, another Act was passed, in connection with the Grand Trunk Railway, at a time when the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was a member of the Laur-ier Administration. This legislatno-n was passed eight or nine months after the agreement was entered into, and while my hon. friend was a member of the Government and of the House. Yet he tells us that it was decided that no legislation would be passed by the Government of which he was a member until these men should be reinstated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will study my remarks carefully, he will see that I spoke of legislation in the nature of financial aid.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
This was all of a financial character. The point is that the leader

of the Opposition endeavoured to lead the House to believe that the Government-of which he was a member refused to pass any legislation unless the Grand Trunk Railway Company should reinstate these men. But here we have two statutes passed, one eight months and another nine months after the agreement was entered into, and no effort was made by the leader of the Opposition to insist upon the Grand Trunk Company doing justice to these men. All he had to do was to appear before the Railway Committee, and ask them not to pass this legislation until the company dealt justly by the men. When I was placed at the head of the Labour Department on the 10th of October, 1911, the evidence was there that there were 200 men who had not been reinstated although one hundred and thirty-eight of them had been declared by the judge to be entitled to be reinstated. Yet they were not reinstated. I went to Charles M. Hays and I said to him in private: "Mr. Hays, you will get no- legislation while this Government is in power until you carry out your agreement respecting these men." At the next session Mr. Wainwright, who was a very fine man, came before the Private Bills Committee and asked to have two Bills sanctioned. I, like the leader of the Opposition, do not care to speak of myself, but I got up and addressed the committee and asked them not to pass these Bills until that agreement was carried out. That is what my hon. friend might have done on the 11th April 1911 and on the 19th May 1911. When I took that [DOT]position Mr. Wainwright reported:	"I
will never make another application to the railway or Private Bills Committee of the House until you carry out that agreement." The result of it was that the agreement was carried out and the men were reinstated or as many of them1 as desired it were reinstated. Some of them had got better jobs elsewhere and they did not desire to be placed back in the employ of the Grand Trunk. Not only were the men received .back into the employ of the company but they got their back pay. I told Mr. Wainwright to send the cheques to me for the back pay; the company sent the cheque -to me and I sent them along. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) who comes from Stafford which is a great Grand Trunk Railway centre, stated the other night that from me these Grand Trunk employees who had been on strike in the city of Stratford received ninety-three cheques some of them for as much as $100. Those were means that the leader of the Opposition might have utilized to force
the Grand Trunk Company to treat these men justly and according to the agreement that they had entered into. Now my hon. friend goes into elaborate, wearying detail, detail that is immaterial, that has nothing whatever to do with the matter, in the effort to make the House believe that he had done everything possible, that no legislation had been, given, and that they had refused to give any money until they had reinstated these men although, as I said, these statutes were passed in May and April of 1911.
Right hon. CHARLES J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice): I have no desire to detain the committee but for a few minutes. I would not do the leader of the Opposition the injustice to imagine, notwithstanding the eloquence to which we have been treated, that he is in the remotest degree serious in the amendment which he has proposed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: What nonsense !

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
II have never in my riot very long parliamentary experience witnessed any such exhibition of childish selfcomplacency and forgetfulness on the part of a gentleman who usually is thoughful of what he owed in common fairness to the members of this Government. He endeavoured in an oration of self-glorification to play upon the natural sympathy of the members of this House for claims that are put forward with very great strength on behalf of a number of workingmen, to pose as their protector and to propose a method of protecting them of which-I will not say, as he said of us with respect to what we said we would do-he knew would produce no effect, I will not say that of him. I will be charitable enough to acknowledge his ignorance that the method he has proposed will produce no effect but that does not alter the fact that he could have selected no less effective a method to be of use to these men if he had made a search to find the most ineffective.
I was lost in adihiration-absolutely lost in admiration-of the honourable leader's capacity for working himself up to a high pitch of indignation when I saw him pounding his fists together. The usually mild leader, in this flood of indignation, could not control himself and had to pound his fists in the fervour of his indignation. Then he told us that justice was eternal,- and justice being eternal he thought it worth while to wait ten years before he would lift a finger to have justice done. He thought it desirable, justice always being eternal and therefore liable to be done by anybody that might come along, to wait not

only ten years but to wait until he had no power to do anything about it; because, you know, justice is eternal and there was lots of time by and by when he would! not be able to do anything about it. Then he would pound his fists and raise himself to a condition of indignation which was almost beyond his own control. I ask you to imagine the lengths to which the leader of the Opposition will go to convince this House that justice is eternal. He would have been willing to have stayed here all night. Surely the workingman population of this great Canada of ours wi carry this heroic figure in triumph.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the minister be prepared to give them a chance?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Most assuredly. It
would afford me the greatest pleasure to convoke a gathering although it will not be needed to be convoked when they read the hon. gentleman's speech and realise that the hon. gentleman would have stayed up all night. They will flock to it and there will be no need for me to intervene.
And then, of course, the hon. gentleman -nobody henceforth can question it-is the most devoted friend of the workingmen. We do not need the evidence of that, it is so unanswerable-the hon. gentleman actually admits it himself. He read us a long letter of his own, irrefutable testimony on the point. I wonder that he found it necessary to read so much of it in view of the fact that we knew who the author was and of course the ipse dixit of the hon. gentleman establishes his qualifications as the sole protector of labour as he was in those days in the past and all through the ten years. And yet he has been doing nothing but biding his time, waiting for the thrilling moment when he would be able to take no action at all except sit up all night. The hon. gentleman himself indicated in the very letter which he read to us to-night, which took so long to read, and w'hich he assured us was going to create a great emotion in the outside world when it was read -il certainly hope it may create a greater commotion outside than it did here, because much to my regret I am forced to confess that I saw some very near neighbours of his who during its reading were giving evidence of how much more profoundly they thought when their eyes were shut-the hon. gentleman, in that very letter pointed out to his leader at that time what he claims he knew ought to have been done, and yet neither his leader nor himself did it. He told his leader that Mr. 
Hays stood behind some provision of the law that prevented his granting these pensions to people who did not have continuous service; and then he went on to point out to his leader that, of course, Parliament had to legislate to confer that power upon the Grand Trunk railway. The hon. gentleman tells us-of course, I do not question the truth of it-that on his own showing at that time he had personal knowledge of all the facts connected with that agreement and its violation. With that knowledge of those facts he was able to lay his finger on the sort of legislation that would have been a complete remedy, and yet neither his leader nor himself-the Government of which they were members continuing in the control of the Parliament of Canada for something approaching two years afterwards-ever moved a finger or took a step to initiate and pass through that legislation which in the hon. gentleman's own letter he points out would have been an effective remedy. Having an absolute knowledge-personal to himself, needing no evidence to bring it to him-of the agreement that had been made and broken and the remedy that could be brought to correct the consequences of it, he folded his arms and did absolutely nothing, and waited as I have said for ten years, to take the action which he has taken to-night.
It is interesting occasionally to look through a little past history. I find that this matter has furnished the subject of discussions in Parliament at an earlier period when the hon. gentleman was in the possession of the power that would have enabled him to enact that legislation that he knew so well was the proper remedy. This matter was discussed at different times, and I find there was a debate with regard to it in the Parliamentary session of 1910-11 which is reported at page 3375 of Hansard. In the course of that discussion the hon. gentleman, who to-day is so full of zeal for the recognition of the claims of these men actually told Parliament-not so long after the events had occurred-that in the course of these negotiations the men said they did not care much about pensions anyway. He was in power then*and he was giving testimony against the claim of the men on whose behalf to-day his heart beats almost to suffocation, on whose behalf his blood boils to the extent that he would sit up all night to effect a settlement. Did he do so at that time when other people were urging the Government to which he belonged to do something? Let me quote

from the hon. gentleman's remarks at that time.
Mr. King: As regards pensions, when the matter was under consideration, the leaders of the men who were negotiating on behalf of the employees took the position that they did not care about pensions one way or the other, that if the company cared to regard them as having violated its agreement with them to the extent of breaking any regulation which governed pensions the company was perfectly free to put that interpretation upon it.
That is the witness for the man talking in 1911 when he had the power to direct such legislation as he might think advisable-that is the testimony he gave at that time. The hon. gentleman said further:
. I -was rather surprised myself at them taking that stand, but they did take it, and they gave me to understand that insofar as pensions were concerned, if they had forfeited the pension by going out, and if the company eared to put that interpretation upon if they were free to do so.
Helpful to the cause of the men, was it not? Helpful to the doing of that justice which' should be rendered.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Who made those remarks?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The Hon. Mr. King, at that time Minister of Labour in the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Now, in view of that record of faithful testimony in the interests of the men and that display of exceeding activity and energy while he was in power, let us look for a moment, at what the hon. gentleman calls upon this Government to do to-day.
As I said a few moments ago, I always think I owe it to myself as a gentleman to impute no dishonest motives to any man, and therefore I will not follow the example which the hon. leader of the Opposition has given us this evening in suggesting that the members of this Government when' they stated what they thought they could do and what they would do knew perfectly well that it would produce no effect. I happen to be the member of the Government who most recently made a statement upon that subject. Of course, henceforth I know in what esteem the hon. leader of the Opposition holds my truthfulness and sincerity. The hon. gentleman's language was not parliamentary but the Speaker did not notice it, and I felt I could treat it with contempt. I will not follow that example, and therefore I will not say that the hon. gentleman is now proposing something which he knows can lead nowhere-his ignorance may earn him forgiveness.
What is it that he proposes we should do now? He proposes that we put in an
agreement, which has been ratified and completed by one of the parties to it, a condition that will, in face of the fact that what is to be done under that agreement is to seek a judicial determination as between us, the acquirers of the company and its present holders, of what are to-day the actual debts of the Grand Trunk-after we have agreed to submit that question to arbitration, my hon. friend proposes that this Parliament shall order that it be made a condition of the agreement that the Grand Trunk Railway Company does owe a certain indebtedness, which up to this time we understand the company has contested.
Certainly hon. members sitting on this side are as anxious to see justice done to those interested in this particular claim as even the hon. gentlemen who sit up all night to say it. But we have got to 'remember that some very elementary general rules bind all persons and all courts,- even this high court of Parliament; and I am satisfied that the very claimants on whose behalf he speaks would recognize, because of the absolute negation of the fundamental principle of British justice that is involved in it, the utter futility and unsusceptibility of justification of the hon. gentleman's proposition. Because, what is it? His proposal is that while he who personally knew the facts at the time when they were fresh, and he had the power to act, would not undertake, or his chief or the Government of which he was a member would not at his instance undertake, to legislate into existence a liability on the part of the Grand Trunk, to-night this- Parliament-proud of being a Parliament that ""carries on'' on the lines of the constitution that we have inherited from the Mother country, and that consequently realizes the absolute injustice and therefore the absolute impossibility under our British system of judging any man or any company unheard,-shall, on the ipse dixit of himself, the great heroic defender of the workingman, proceeds to do what he did not venture to do with his own personal knowledge. In effect, he says:	You shall proceed to
decide that question with regard to each and every one of those men and the company.
Now, I have read and, only the other day, I heard very strong expressions of a conviction that the claims of the men were well founded. I am very strongly impressed that they are right. But I cannot say that I have the proof. The hon. gentleman says he has the proof,-and he had it in time and would not use it. I have not got the

proof, none of us sitting on this side of the House has got the proof, that would justify us to determine that question to-night in one sense or the other and constitute ourselves a court of justice to do what no court of justice in any British land would dream of doing-condemn a party without having heard him. That is what the hon. gentleman asks us to do. It is said, -that where ignorance is bliss 'tis folly to be wise. Certainly, fortunate is he who can save himself from the criticism of such a proposal by the all-covering mantle of ab-sense of knowledge and of appreciation of the most elementary and fundamental principles that ought to guide a public man in dealing with public questions.
Now,-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext: As a matter of correct statement I want to say a word to my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext: Certainly, if the hon. gentleman wants to interrupt me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
