speechtext: I thought my right hon. friend was through.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Now, let me call attention to another matter. I think I have made sufficiently clear to any one except the hon. gentleman the manifest impossibility of there being any way out in the direction he has chosen for the protection of those whom he has taken under his care. I heard a learned judge once open his charge to a jury by saying, "Gentlemen of the jury, the prisoner at the bar has had the disadvantage of counsel.'' I wish to point out some of the things-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: What.would have happened to him if he had been defended by the Minister of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT.
subtopic: BILL TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
My good and honourable friend knows better than that, and he is well enough acquainted with me to know that nothing he could say would annoy me, because I know and appreciate the goodness and kindness of his heart. I do not make the observation in any offensive way.
Now, as I have said, I think I have made sufficiently clear the impossibility of applying the particular remedy which counsel on behalf of these men-self-constituted counsel-under the disadvantage of whose advocacy they suffer, has suggested for them.
But let us suppose for a moment that it were an adaquate remedy and that the hon. gentleman had always thought, as he thtinks to-night, that it was an adequate remedy, and that all through these ten years, as

he has represented, he has toiled and sat up long nights nursing the one consolation of the knowledge that "justice is eternal," and nursing and keeping warm his adamantine determination that if the day ever came when he could do nothing about the matter he would-make trouble for somebody else. 'What is the situation? Included in that long period of ten years was the session last fall. The hon. gentleman was not with us during that session so long as, perhaps, he would have liked to have been. I am sure we would have all been glad to have him with us sooner,- not that we would not have regretted seeing the diminution of authority of the authority of the hon. gentleman whom he replaced. But he (Mr. Mackenzie King) was in this House a very considerable part of that session, long enough to make speeches about the Bill that was before the House and about the agreement that >vas to be made. During all that time his mind was filled with the reflection that "justice is eternal" and that justice must be done, and that the way to do justice was to put into that agreeement the clause that he proposes to-night. But instead of .putting it in, he sat by and heard set forth and passed into law every precise thing that was to be put into that agreement; he sat by, this heroic self-saerificer in the interest of justice, and treasured up ,and kept well within his bosom that knowledge of which he had the monopoly that in this little clause in that agreement was justice for the workingman. But he never proposed it in useful time, when Parli-ment was determining, before the agreement was drawn up, what ought to be put .into it, and when Parliament was agreed, that when the agreement as authorized by this Parliament would be drawn up and ratified by the Government, that would be the agreement. During all that time we never heard a whisper of this talismanic clause that was to ensure justice to the .workingman. It was carefully hoarded up until it was too late to be useful to the workingman, but might, perhaps, serve some purpose in putting a difficulty in the way of the passing of this measure which has not the remotest conneection with anything of that kind, and might, perhaps, furnish to the future historian an opportunity of admiring my hon. friend's magnificent flow of eloquence including the reading-which did not flow quite so smoothly -to which we were listening this evening.
It is remarkable that during those ten years that there should have been a moment

of forgetfulness, a sort of interlude that occurred during that period of last session when the hon. gentleman was here, when this great duty of seeing that justice should ,be done, when he was in a better position to do it, escaped his attention; or, perhaps, after all, as hon. members know, may happen when one hugs to his bosom the-belief, which affords such gratification to the hon. pose it was another case of thinking there was no hurry. Just as there was no hurry when he could have done something, so there was no hurry last session when he could have done something if this amendment to the agreement would be effective in doing anything in any event. But he did not do it then-apparently the thought about justice being eternal did not press strongly on him at the moment. Perhaps he thought then he had some other ways of embarrassing the passing of this measure. To-night, however, he has waked up and he has revived this letter of which he has given us the benefit. I am not going to try the experiment; but it would be a very interesting one, to try to see which would be the more tiresome-to sit and listen to that letter, or to sit down and endeavour to read it. I should like to have a committee consider that point and make a report. I suppose the hon. member flatters himself that that letter is going to produce a commotion from one end of this great Dominion to the other and to settle forever, on the strength of his own testimony, that we have in him the greatest friend of labour, the greatest settler of labour's disputes, that Canada or any other country ever knew. He counts on that letter, and this little amendment looks to- me very like an excuse, a something on which to hang that letter and the .accompanying speech, and to enable the hon. gentleman to get himself properly reposed on that pedestal of Saviour of Labour, upon w'hich he disported himself so gracefully this evening.
I do not know that it was necessary to enter into a discussion of this thing. As I said at the outset I cannot really bring myself to do the hon. gentleman's intelligence the injustice of believing that he is ,really serious in this matter. It has served his purposes. He has made his speech; he has read his letter; he has posed as Labour's saviour; he has thrilled us through and through with the novel statement that "justice is eternal," and he has given us a super-thrill as we stood and watched and listened to him making that heroic declaration, which I have no doubt will be his-87
toric, that when justice is at stake, he is /willing to stay up all night. Surely his purpose has 'been achieved. Any man who, with a little amendment of that kind, can achieve all that, ought to be able to go home and sleep quite quietly and think in the few hours between now and morning Justice can take care of herself.
I do not know whether I am right or wrong in my opinion of how seriously the hon. gentleman takes this resolution. I have no doubt at all that the common sense of the committee does not take this amendment as meaning anything serious, and I am equally satisfied that it will entirely fail of what, I will not say was its deliberate purpose, but as I look at it, this is its only possible explanation-of casting dust- in the eyes of the workingmen of this country and inducing them to take the exhibition of this evening as having any serious meaning and as an attempt to be of service to them.
Now let me come back for a moment to what I said the other day; at the risk of the imputation of dishonesty or insincerity, I propose to repeat it. Do you serve people by showy speeches and means that bring you nowhere? Or do you serve people by giving them the best assistance that can he given without asking for violation of the most ordinary principles which govern the determination of claims of one person against an other? I did say the other day, and other colleagues of mine have said before, that they would see to it that fair opportunity was given for fair and just hearing of the representations 'that can be made on behalf of the men. I am sure that the testimony of the hon. member will be invoked for its full value. I would hope that in some way the testimony that he gave in 1911 in the days of his power would be overlooked. As to his testimony of to-night in that lengthy letter-well, perhaps he will have a committee appointed to make a digest of it, and when it is properly digested I have no doubt that it will be more effective. However that may he, when I say things I am in the habit of saying things that I mean. I am not habituated to being told that the things I say I know mean nothing, I say again that every possible opportunity of putting the claims of these men in shape to be property passed upon by a competent authority, namely, by the Board of Arbitration, who will have opportunity of hearing both sides, will be given.
I shall not go into what may happen if there is found to he no legal claim, but a moral claim, or what may be the conse-



quences if there is found to be a legal claim. That opportunity will be afforded, as I said the other day, and if that means should pr6ve ineffective, then it will be for the Government of that time-whether the sins of this country should put it in certain hands that aspire to grasp it or whether it remains where it is-to determine what the justice and the equity of the case calls-for. For my part, in view of the heroics of the hon. gentleman, I would rather the people of Canada paid that money, if it ought to be paid and if it be impossible to establish the liability of the Grand Trunk for it, than ask the people of Canada through their representatives to prostitute the authority that this Parliament has by attempting to pronounce judgment in a case which it has never heard-a violation of everything that is associated with the commonest idea of justice. It is the boast of the British people that that is the one fundamental thing that cannot be tolerated under any system where British justice is administered. That is the proposal; that is the only method that the hon. gentleman has to propose to meet this evil. I have only to ask the committee, in the light in which I am sure this amendment must present itself to them, to vote it down I had almost said to laugh it down.

I ask hon.
gentlemen to permit me to make this statement. There will be no doubt as to the connection in which my statement was made. The point with regard to pensions was this: Mr. Lennox, at that time a member of the House, had asked whether the Government were not responsible in connection with the men not getting their pensions. Answer was made through a letter from one of the strike leaders in which he directed particular attention to the fact

that the matter of pensions was not discussed one way or the other at the conferences with the company. My statement has been on record and has never been taken exception to by the men. What I have said to-night has related to conferences between the company and the employees. The subject was never mentioned alt the conferences, buit apart from the conferences the strike leaders said to me-and I think they would say it Ito-day-that they did not believe in the business of pensions with companies, and the reason is found in the example given by this company: the pensions are used by companies as manacles upon freedom rather than as rewards for service. That is the connection in which I said I was surprised that the strike leaders took that position in regard to pensions. But when it comes to the obligation of the company, the company is bound in the agreement that they entered into with the leaders by what the understanding was at the table around which the discussion took , place. Certainly the understanding there was that the men should go back on the same status which they had before, and to the same positions. To my way of thinking, that includes pensions, whether the strike leaders wish it or not.

speechtext: I want to suggest that there is no use in our sitting here for hours continuing this discussion. If hon. members on either side wish to speak further, the proper and sensible thing is for the committee to rise. My experience of alknight sessions has been that when we wake up the next morning we come to the conclusion that we hiad been playing a very foolish part. If the matter is to he the occasion of further discussion', I suggest that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
